# MOONX guides, full text

> Every guide published on https://moonx.fi/learn/, in Markdown. Updated 2026-10-27.

# What is a prediction market? A plain-English guide

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-is-a-prediction-market
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: A prediction market is a market where people buy and sell shares in the answer to a real question, like "Will Bitcoin be above $100,000 on Friday?". Each share costs between 1¢ and 99¢. If your answer is right, every share pays $1. If it's wrong, it pays nothing. The price is the crowd's best guess of the odds: 30¢ means about a 30% chance.

## The idea in one example

Take a question: **"Will it rain in London tomorrow?"** Two answers are possible, Yes and No. People who think it will rain buy Yes. People who think it won't buy No.

Say Yes trades at **70¢** and No at **30¢**. The two always add up to about $1, because exactly one of them will be right. When tomorrow comes and it rains, every Yes share pays **$1** and every No share pays **$0**.

::: ex Worked example
You buy 10 Yes shares at 70¢. You spend **$7**. If it rains, you get **$10** back, a profit of $3. If it doesn't rain, your shares are worth nothing and you lose the $7.

Someone else buys 10 No shares at 30¢ and spends **$3**. If it stays dry, they get **$10**, more than three times their money. If it rains, they lose $3.
:::

That's the whole mechanism. Everything else, fees, selling early, multi-outcome markets, builds on it.

## What the price tells you

The price of a share is the market's estimate of the chance that it wins. At 70¢, buyers and sellers agree, for now, that rain is about 70% likely. If a weather update makes rain look certain, people rush to buy Yes and the price climbs toward 99¢. If the clouds clear, it falls.

This is why prediction markets get quoted in the news. A price is a number that people backed with their own money, and it updates within seconds when something happens. Academic work going back two decades, such as [Wolfers and Zitzewitz (2004)](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/0895330041371321), found that market prices are often good forecasts, though not perfect ones.

To turn any price into odds and a payout, see [prediction market odds, explained](/learn/prediction-market-odds).

## Who is on the other side of your trade?

Other people. A prediction market is a marketplace, not a bookmaker. When you buy Yes at 70¢, someone else is buying No at 30¢, or selling you Yes shares they already own. The price comes from all those orders meeting in an **order book**.

This has two consequences:

- Nobody sets the odds against you. There is no house margin built into the price. Platforms earn through a trading fee instead, and on Polymarket that fee depends on the market (see [Polymarket fees, explained](/learn/polymarket-fees)).
- You can **sell your shares before the result** to anyone who wants to buy them. If you bought at 20¢ and the price is now 60¢, you can take that gain today without waiting. More on that in [selling before the result](/learn/sell-before-the-result).

## What kinds of questions can you trade?

Almost anything with a clear answer and a date. On [Polymarket](https://polymarket.com), one of the largest prediction markets, you will find:

- **Sports:** who wins a match, a league, a title.
- **Crypto:** where Bitcoin or Ethereum will be at a given time.
- **Politics and elections:** who wins, by how much, what passes.
- **News and culture:** awards, product launches, box office, weather.

Some questions have only Yes and No. Others have many possible answers, like "Who will win the Ballon d'Or?". Those work a little differently, explained in [multi-outcome markets](/learn/multi-outcome-markets).

## How does a market end?

Every market has written rules: what counts as Yes, which source decides, and when. When the event is over, the result is proposed and checked, then winning shares pay $1. On Polymarket this is done through an independent system called the UMA Optimistic Oracle, with a challenge window before anything is final. The full process is in [how Polymarket markets are resolved](/learn/how-polymarket-resolves-markets).

Read the rules before you trade. A market called "Will X happen by June?" might count only an official announcement, not a rumour. Most surprises come from rules people skipped.

## What can you lose?

Only what you put in. A share can go to zero, never below. There is no leverage and no margin call on a regular prediction market trade: $10 in means at most $10 at risk.

::: risk The honest part
Cheap shares pay big because they usually lose. A 5¢ share pays 20 times your money when it wins, and the market thinks it wins about 1 time in 20. Only put in money you can lose without it changing anything in your life.
:::

## Common questions {faq}

### Is a prediction market the same as betting?

They look alike, but the mechanics differ. You trade with other people at a price that moves, and you can sell before the end. A bookmaker sets the odds and is the other side of your bet. Whether a country treats prediction markets as financial trading or as gambling depends on its own rules. We compare both in [prediction markets vs sports betting](/learn/prediction-markets-vs-sports-betting).

### Do I need crypto to use a prediction market?

Polymarket settles trades in a dollar token on the Polygon network, so behind the scenes it is crypto. Apps built on Polymarket, like MOONX, can hide that part: you sign up with an email and add money with a card.

### How much money do I need to start?

Very little. Each market sets a minimum order size, and on many markets a trade starts at around a dollar.

### Why do Yes and No add up to $1?

Because one of them will pay $1 and the other $0. If Yes costs 70¢, a No share that pays $1 in the other case is worth about 30¢. In practice there is a small gap between the best buy and sell prices, called the spread.

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: prices and the order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
2. [Polymarket documentation: resolution](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/resolution)
3. [Wolfers, J. and Zitzewitz, E. (2004), Prediction Markets, Journal of Economic Perspectives](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/0895330041371321)

# How does Polymarket work? Shares, prices and payouts

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/how-polymarket-works
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: On Polymarket, every question has Yes and No shares priced between 0 and $1. You buy from other traders through an order book, you can sell any time before the end, and when the market resolves each winning share pays $1. The price shown is usually the middle of the best buy and sell offers, so the price you actually pay can be a little higher.

## The short version

1. Each market asks a question with a deadline and written rules.
2. You buy **Yes** or **No** shares. Each share pays **$1** if it's right, **$0** if it's wrong.
3. Prices move between 0 and $1 as people trade. The price reads as a probability: 25¢ means about 25%.
4. You can sell your shares to other traders at any time before the market ends.
5. When the answer is known, the market resolves and winning shares pay out.

The rest of this guide explains each step and the details that trip people up.

## Yes and No are two sides of one dollar

On Polymarket, a Yes share and a No share together are always worth exactly $1, because one of them will pay. That's why their prices mirror each other. Polymarket's own documentation gives the example of a Yes buyer at 60¢ being matched with a No buyer at 40¢: together they put up $1, and each receives their share.

In practice this means "buy No at 40¢" and "sell Yes at 60¢" are almost the same trade. You don't need to understand it to trade, but it explains why Yes and No prices always add up to roughly $1.

## The price you see, and the price you pay

Polymarket runs an **order book**. Buyers post the highest price they are willing to pay (the bid). Sellers post the lowest price they will accept (the ask). The gap between them is the **spread**.

According to Polymarket's documentation, the price displayed on a market is the **midpoint** of the best bid and best ask. If the spread is wider than 10¢, it shows the last traded price instead.

::: ex Worked example
The best bid for Yes is 34¢ and the best ask is 40¢. The market shows **37¢**, the midpoint.

If you buy right now, you pay the ask: **40¢**. If you sell right now, you get the bid: **34¢**. Buy and immediately sell, and you lose 6¢ a share before any fee.
:::

On busy markets the spread is often a single tick, so the difference is small. On quiet markets it can be wide. Always look at the price on the buy button, not just the headline number.

## Market orders and limit orders

There are two ways to trade:

- A **market order** fills right away against the best offers in the book. You get speed, but if your order is large compared with what's available, part of it can fill at worse prices.
- A **limit order** sets the worst price you will accept. It can sit in the book until someone takes it, or until you cancel it.

MOONX keeps this simple: you choose Yes or No and an amount, you see the price and the cost, and you confirm.

## Minimums and sizes

Each Polymarket market sets its own minimum order size, counted in shares, and its own **tick size** (the smallest price step, often 1¢, sometimes smaller). The minimum is counted in shares, so on many markets a trade can start at around a dollar.

## What you hold, and where

Your shares are tokens on the **Polygon** blockchain. Polymarket settles trades in **pUSD**, a dollar token backed by USDC that it introduced in 2026 to replace the bridged USDC it used before. When you sell, or when you win, you receive dollars back.

Because everything is on a public blockchain, every trade is visible. That's why you can look up any trader's positions, and why apps can show you what other people are trading.

## How a market ends

When the event is over, someone proposes the result and posts a bond. If nobody disputes it within **2 hours**, the result stands and winning shares can be redeemed for $1 each. Disputes go through a longer process, typically 4 to 6 days, run by the UMA Optimistic Oracle. Short crypto "Up or Down" markets settle automatically from a Chainlink price feed instead. The details are in [how Polymarket markets are resolved](/learn/how-polymarket-resolves-markets).

## What it costs

On most markets, the trader who takes an existing offer pays a **taker fee** that depends on the category and on the price. Some categories, such as geopolitics, have no fee. Deposits and withdrawals are free on Polymarket's side. The full table, with examples in cents, is in [Polymarket fees, explained](/learn/polymarket-fees).

## Where apps like MOONX fit in

Polymarket runs a **Builders Program**: apps that send their users' orders to Polymarket and are credited for that volume. The markets, the prices and the settlement are Polymarket's. The app decides how it looks, how you sign up and how you hold your money.

MOONX is one of these apps. You sign up with an email, you add money with a card or with USDC, and your wallet is created on your own device, so only you can move your money. Your trades go to Polymarket, and your winnings come back to the same wallet. The difference is mostly in the experience: a social feed of real trades, no seed phrase to write down, and no network fees to pay. You can read the whole flow in [your first trade on MOONX](/learn/first-trade-on-moonx).

## Common questions {faq}

### Is Polymarket a bookmaker?

No. Polymarket doesn't set odds or take the other side of your trade. Prices come from traders buying and selling with each other in an order book.

### Can I sell before the market ends?

Yes, at any time, as long as someone is willing to buy. On busy markets that is instant. On quiet ones you may have to accept a lower price. See [selling before the result](/learn/sell-before-the-result).

### What happens to my money if I'm right?

Each winning share pays $1 when the market resolves. If you bought 50 Yes shares at 20¢ for $10 and Yes wins, you receive $50.

### Is Polymarket available everywhere?

No. Polymarket blocks or restricts access in a number of countries, and the list changes. MOONX follows Polymarket's restrictions and adds a few of its own, listed in its [Terms](/terms). Check the rules where you live before you trade.

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: prices and the order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
2. [Polymarket documentation: placing orders, order types and sizes](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/place-orders)
3. [Polymarket documentation: resolution](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/resolution)
4. [Polymarket documentation: Builders Program](https://docs.polymarket.com/programs/builders/overview)
5. [Polymarket documentation: pUSD](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/pusd)

# Prediction market odds: how a price becomes a payout

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/prediction-market-odds
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Divide $1 by the price to get your payout multiple. A share at 20¢ pays $1, so it returns 5x your money if you're right, and the market gives it about a 20% chance. At 50¢ it's 2x, at 5¢ it's 20x, at 90¢ it's about 1.11x. Fees and the spread lower the real multiple a little.

## Three numbers from one price

Every share on Polymarket pays **$1** if it's right. So the price alone tells you three things:

- **Implied probability:** the price in cents is the chance in percent. 20¢ is about 20%.
- **Payout multiple:** $1 divided by the price. 20¢ gives 1 ÷ 0.20 = **5x**.
- **What $10 becomes:** $10 buys 10 ÷ 0.20 = 50 shares, which pay **$50** if you're right.

The multiple is also what sports bettors call **decimal odds**. A 5x share is the same as odds of 5.00.

## The table

| Price | Implied chance | Multiple | $10 returns | American odds |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1¢ | 1% | 100x | $1,000 | +9900 |
| 5¢ | 5% | 20x | $200 | +1900 |
| 10¢ | 10% | 10x | $100 | +900 |
| 20¢ | 20% | 5x | $50 | +400 |
| 25¢ | 25% | 4x | $40 | +300 |
| 33¢ | 33% | 3.03x | $30.30 | +203 |
| 50¢ | 50% | 2x | $20 | +100 |
| 60¢ | 60% | 1.67x | $16.67 | -150 |
| 75¢ | 75% | 1.33x | $13.33 | -300 |
| 90¢ | 90% | 1.11x | $11.11 | -900 |
| 95¢ | 95% | 1.05x | $10.53 | -1900 |

Amounts are before fees. "$10 returns" is the total you get back if you're right, your $10 included.

## The formulas

If the price is **p** (in dollars, so 20¢ is 0.20):

- Multiple, or decimal odds: **1 ÷ p**
- Shares you get for an amount: **amount ÷ p**
- Profit if you're right: **amount × (1 ÷ p − 1)**
- American odds: if p is 0.50 or under, **+100 × (1 − p) ÷ p**. If p is over 0.50, **−100 × p ÷ (1 − p)**.

## When is a trade worth taking?

A price is the market's estimate. You only have an edge if you think the real chance is higher than the price.

::: ex Worked example
A share trades at **20¢**. You believe the real chance is **30%**.

For every $1 you put in, you get 5 shares. On average you expect 30% × $5 = **$1.50** back. That's a positive expected value of 50¢ per dollar, before fees.

If you think the real chance is 15%, the same trade expects 15% × $5 = $0.75 back per dollar. You would be paying for a long shot that's priced too high.
:::

This is the only test that matters, and it's humbling. The market price already combines what thousands of people know. Beating it on a regular basis is hard.

## Why the real multiple is a bit lower

Four things sit between the table and your result:

1. **The spread.** You buy at the ask, which can be a cent or more above the price on the screen. At low prices a cent matters a lot: buying at 6¢ instead of 5¢ turns 20x into 16.7x.
2. **Polymarket's taker fee.** On most markets, an order that fills right away pays a fee. As a share of the money you spend, it works out to the fee rate times (1 − price). On a crypto market (rate 0.07), buying at 20¢ costs about 5.6% of your stake. At 90¢ it's 0.7%. Geopolitics markets have no fee. Details in [Polymarket fees, explained](/learn/polymarket-fees).
3. **The app's fee.** MOONX charges 1% of the trade value when you buy and when you sell. There is no fee when a market resolves.
4. **Time.** Your money is tied up until the market ends. A 90¢ share that pays $1 in a year is a different deal from one that pays tomorrow.

::: ex Worked example: fees included
$10 on Yes at **20¢** on a crypto market: 50 shares. Polymarket's fee is about $0.56 and MOONX's is $0.10, so the trade costs you about **$10.66** in all. If Yes wins you receive **$50**: a multiple of about **4.7x** instead of 5x. Numbers are rounded, and the app shows the exact amounts before you confirm.
:::

## Selling early changes the math

You don't have to wait for $1. If you bought at 20¢ and the price climbs to 60¢, you can sell and take **3x** right away, whatever happens next. On MOONX that's one button, Eject. Many good trades are closed this way. See [selling before the result](/learn/sell-before-the-result).

## Common questions {faq}

### What do Polymarket odds mean?

The price of a share is the market's estimate of the probability. Yes at 35¢ means traders, as a group, put the chance at about 35%.

### How do I calculate my payout on Polymarket?

Divide the amount you put in by the price to get your number of shares. Each share pays $1 if you're right. $25 at 40¢ is 62.5 shares, so $62.50 if you win, before fees.

### Are cheap shares a better deal?

Not by default. A 5¢ share pays 20x, but the market thinks it wins about 1 time in 20. Studies of betting and prediction markets often find long shots slightly overpriced. Read [long shots on Polymarket](/learn/long-shot-trades) before you chase them.

### Why do Yes and No not add up to exactly $1?

Because of the spread. The best ask for Yes plus the best ask for No is usually a cent or two above $1. That gap is what you pay to trade instantly.

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: prices and the order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
2. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)
3. [MOONX Terms of Service, section 11: fees](/terms)

# Polymarket fees explained, with real numbers

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/polymarket-fees
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: On most Polymarket markets, the trader whose order fills right away (the taker) pays a fee of shares × rate × price × (1 − price). Rates go from 0 for geopolitics to 0.07 for crypto. As a share of the money you spend, that's the rate times (1 − price): about 3.5% at 50¢ on a crypto market, 2.5% on sports, 2% on politics. Makers pay nothing, and there is no fee when a market resolves.

## Who pays, and when

Polymarket uses an order book. Some orders wait in the book (they **make** liquidity). Others fill against them right away (they **take** liquidity). According to Polymarket's documentation, **takers pay a fee on most markets and makers pay none**. The fee is applied when the trade matches, in dollars.

There is no fee when a market resolves and your winning shares pay $1. Polymarket also charges nothing to deposit or withdraw, though the service you use to move money may charge its own fee.

## The formula

For a trade of **C** shares at a price **p**:

`fee = C × rate × p × (1 − p)`

Because of the p × (1 − p) part, the fee in dollars is highest at 50¢ and shrinks toward the extremes. There is a simpler way to read it: divided by what you spend (C × p), the fee is just **rate × (1 − p)** of your stake.

## The rate for each category

| Category | Taker rate | Fee at 50¢, per 100 shares |
|---|---:|---:|
| Crypto | 0.07 | $1.75 |
| Sports | 0.05 | $1.25 |
| Economics, culture, weather, other | 0.05 | $1.25 |
| Finance, politics, tech, mentions | 0.04 | $1.00 |
| Combos (several outcomes in one trade) | 0.05 | $1.25 |
| Geopolitics and world events | 0 | $0 |

Rates as published in Polymarket's fee documentation, checked on 27 October 2026. Polymarket can change them, so check its page before relying on a number.

## What you pay, as a percentage

This is the table most people actually want: the fee as a share of the money you put in.

| Price you buy at | Crypto | Sports | Politics |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 5¢ | 6.65% | 4.75% | 3.80% |
| 20¢ | 5.60% | 4.00% | 3.20% |
| 50¢ | 3.50% | 2.50% | 2.00% |
| 80¢ | 1.40% | 1.00% | 0.80% |
| 95¢ | 0.35% | 0.25% | 0.20% |

The pattern matters: **cheap shares carry the highest fee in percentage terms.** A long shot on a crypto market costs almost 7% of your stake to enter. A near-certain favourite costs a fraction of a percent. When you sell, the same rule applies to what you receive.

## A full example, from buy to sell

::: ex Worked example
You put **$20** on Yes at **50¢** in a football market. You get **40 shares**.

- Polymarket fee: 40 × 0.05 × 0.50 × 0.50 = **$0.50**
- MOONX fee, 1% of $20: **$0.20**

Total fees to get in: about **$0.70**.

**If you hold and Yes wins:** you receive $40, with no fee at resolution. Fees included, your profit is about **$19.30**.

**If you sell at 70¢ before the end:** 40 shares bring in $28. Polymarket's fee is 40 × 0.05 × 0.70 × 0.30 = $0.42 and MOONX's is $0.28, so you receive about **$27.30**. Your profit is about **$6.60**, locked in whatever happens next. Numbers are rounded, and the app shows the exact amounts before you confirm.
:::

## Ways the fee gets smaller

- **Higher prices cost less.** As a share of your stake, the fee is rate × (1 − price), so it shrinks as the price rises toward $1. Cheap long shots carry the biggest fee.
- **Geopolitics is free.** Those markets carry no taker fee.
- **Make instead of take.** On Polymarket directly, a limit order that waits in the book pays no fee, and makers can earn rebates. The trade-off is that it may never fill.
- **Hold to the end.** If you're confident, holding to resolution avoids the fee on the way out.

Polymarket also runs a Taker Rebate Program that returns part of the fees to active traders, in tiers. See its documentation for the current levels.

## What MOONX adds

MOONX charges **1% of the trade value** when you buy and when you sell, and shows the full cost before you confirm. There is **no fee when a market resolves**, no subscription, no account fee and no withdrawal fee. MOONX also pays the network (gas) fees on your transactions, so you never need to hold another token. Card payment partners may charge their own fee when you add money.

Part of MOONX's fee goes back to users: if a friend joins through your link, you earn 25% of MOONX's fee on their trades. More in [earn with MOONX](/learn/earn-with-moonx).

## Common questions {faq}

### Does Polymarket charge a fee to withdraw?

No. Polymarket charges nothing to deposit or withdraw. The exchange, card provider or bridge you use may charge its own fee.

### Do I pay a fee if I win?

No. Fees are charged when a trade matches, on the way in and on the way out if you sell. When a market resolves, winning shares pay $1 each with no fee.

### Why is the fee bigger on cheap shares?

In dollars it isn't: it peaks at 50¢. But as a percentage of what you spend it's the rate times (1 − price), so a 5¢ share pays close to the full rate.

### Which Polymarket markets have no fee?

Geopolitics and world events markets have a taker rate of zero, according to Polymarket's documentation.

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)
2. [Polymarket documentation: Maker Rebates Program](https://docs.polymarket.com/programs/maker-rebates)
3. [Polymarket documentation: Taker Rebate Program](https://docs.polymarket.com/programs/taker-rebates)
4. [MOONX Terms of Service, section 11: fees](/terms)

# How Polymarket markets are resolved, and what happens in a dispute

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/how-polymarket-resolves-markets
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Most Polymarket markets are resolved through the UMA Optimistic Oracle. After the event, someone proposes the result and posts a bond, typically $750. If nobody disputes it within 2 hours, it's final and winning shares pay $1. A dispute adds a second round and, if needed, a vote by UMA token holders, which takes about 4 to 6 days in total. Short crypto Up or Down markets settle automatically from a Chainlink price feed.

## It starts with the rules

Every Polymarket market has written rules under its order book: what counts as Yes, what source is used, and the deadline. The result is judged against those rules, not against what most people expected. If a market asks whether something is "officially announced by March 31", a credible leak on March 30 doesn't count.

Reading the rules takes a minute and prevents the most common bad surprise.

## Step by step: an undisputed result

1. **The event happens.** The market stops making sense to trade once the answer is known.
2. **Someone proposes the result.** The proposer posts a bond, typically **$750**, through the UMA Optimistic Oracle.
3. **A 2-hour challenge window opens.** Anyone who thinks the proposal is wrong can dispute it during this time.
4. **No dispute, so the result stands.** The proposer gets the bond back plus a reward. Trading stops, winning shares are worth **$1** and losing shares **$0**.

In the normal case, the whole thing takes about two hours after the proposal. The bond is what keeps it honest: proposing a wrong result means losing the $750 bond, half of which goes to whoever proves it wrong.

## When someone disagrees

A dispute also costs a bond of the same size. Then:

- **First dispute:** the proposal is thrown out and a new round of proposals starts.
- **Second dispute:** the question goes to UMA's Data Verification Mechanism (DVM), where UMA token holders vote. Evidence is discussed in UMA's public Discord channels, during a debate period of 24 to 48 hours. The vote itself takes about 48 hours.

Polymarket's documentation puts the full disputed timeline at **4 to 6 days**. Whoever wins gets their bond back plus half of the other side's.

::: note What a dispute means for you
Your shares stay in your wallet the whole time. Nothing is paid out until the final result, so a dispute can delay your money by several days. The written rules of the market are what the voters judge, which is one more reason to read them before you trade.
:::

## The rare outcomes

- **"Too early":** if a result is proposed before the event has really happened, it's rejected.
- **50-50:** if the question can't be answered under its rules, the market can resolve "Unknown", and each share redeems for **$0.50**, whichever side you held.
- **Clarifications:** in rare cases Polymarket publishes "additional context" on a market. It can't change the market's basic intent, it's recorded on the blockchain, and UMA voters are expected to take it into account.

## Up or Down markets settle differently

Short crypto markets, such as "Will Bitcoin be up or down in the next 15 minutes?", don't go through proposals. They settle automatically from a **Chainlink** price feed: Up if the final price is equal to or greater than the starting price, Down if it's lower. No bond, no dispute.

## What you need to do when you win

On Polymarket, winning shares become redeemable for $1 each once the market resolves. On MOONX you don't need to do anything: once the market settles, the money lands in the wallet you traded from, usually within a few minutes, sometimes a few hours. It happens on-chain, so you can watch it.

## Common questions {faq}

### Who decides the outcome of a Polymarket market?

Not Polymarket. Most markets are resolved through the UMA Optimistic Oracle: a proposer posts a bond, anyone can dispute within 2 hours, and contested cases go to a vote of UMA token holders.

### How long does Polymarket take to pay out?

About 2 hours after a result is proposed, if nobody disputes it. A disputed market takes about 4 to 6 days.

### Can a Polymarket result be wrong?

It can be contested, and in rare cases the outcome surprises traders who didn't read the rules closely. The bond system makes a deliberately wrong proposal expensive, but the vote is still a human process.

### What happens if a market is cancelled or unclear?

If the question can't be answered under its rules, it can resolve 50-50 and every share pays $0.50.

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: resolution](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/resolution)
2. [Polymarket Help Center: how are prediction markets resolved?](https://help.polymarket.com/en/articles/13364518-how-are-prediction-markets-resolved)

# Selling before the result: take profit or cut a loss on Polymarket

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/sell-before-the-result
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Yes. Polymarket shares can be sold at any time before the market resolves, to anyone who wants to buy them. You get the current bid price, minus fees. If you bought at 10¢ and the price is now 40¢, you can sell for about 4x your money today, without waiting to see who is right. On quiet markets a sale can take longer or need a lower price.

## You can be wrong and still make money

This is the part that surprises people. Say you buy Yes at **10¢** on a team to win the league. Halfway through the season they are top of the table and Yes trades at **40¢**. You sell. You have made **4x**, before fees. If the team collapses in the last month, you don't care: you already sold.

The reverse works too. If the news turns against you, selling at 4¢ what you bought at 10¢ gets you 40% of your money back. Waiting might get you zero.

## What price you get

When you sell straight away, your shares fill against the best **bids** in the order book, the highest prices other traders are offering. That's a little below the price shown on the market, which is usually the midpoint between bids and asks.

- On busy markets the gap is often a single tick, and a sale is instant.
- On quiet markets the best bid can be several cents lower, and there may not be enough buyers for all your shares at one price. You can wait, or accept a lower price.

Fees apply on the way out too: Polymarket's taker fee where the category has one, and on MOONX, 1% of the amount. See [Polymarket fees](/learn/polymarket-fees).

::: ex Worked example
You bought **100 shares** of Yes at **12¢**: $12. The market now shows 47¢, with the best bid at **46¢**.

Selling all 100 at 46¢ brings in **$46**. On a sports market, Polymarket's fee is 100 × 0.05 × 0.46 × 0.54 = about $1.24, and MOONX's is $0.46. You keep about **$44.30**. Counting the fees you paid to buy, about $0.65, that's roughly **3.5x** your money, locked in.
:::

## When selling early makes sense

- **The price has moved a lot in your favour.** Going from 10¢ to 50¢ is 5x. Going from 50¢ to $1 is only 2x more, and that last part carries all the risk of being wrong. Many traders take part or all of the gain here.
- **Your reason for the trade is gone.** You bought because a player was fit, and now he's injured. The original idea no longer holds, so the position has no reason to stay.
- **You need the money for something else.** Money in a market that ends in six months is money you can't use.
- **The market is about to become volatile.** Before a debate, a match or a court ruling, prices can jump either way in minutes.

## When holding makes sense

- **You still think the real chance is higher than the price.** That's the only good reason to hold. At 90¢, holding to $1 is worth it only if you're more than 90% sure.
- **The share is almost at $1.** Near the end, selling at 97¢ removes only 3¢ of risk per share and still costs a sell fee.

## Selling part of a position

You don't have to choose all or nothing. A common approach: sell enough to get back what you put in, and let the rest ride for free. If you bought 100 shares at 20¢ ($20) and the price is 50¢, selling 40 shares returns about $20. The other 60 shares cost you nothing now.

## Selling on MOONX

On MOONX, each position has an **Eject** button. One tap sells at the best price on the book. MOONX shows the price and the fee before you confirm. On a quiet or fast-moving market, the price can come out lower, and a sale can fill only partly. The money comes back to your wallet. There's no lock-up and no withdrawal fee.

## Common questions {faq}

### Can you cash out early on Polymarket?

Yes. You can sell your shares to other traders at any time before the market resolves, at the current bid price.

### Why did I get less than the price shown?

The price on the market is usually the midpoint between the best bid and the best ask. Selling right away fills at the bid, which is lower, and fees are taken from the amount.

### What if nobody wants to buy my shares?

On very quiet markets there may be few buyers. You can post a sale at a higher price and wait, or lower your price. On busy markets this is rarely a problem.

### Is it better to sell or hold until the end?

Hold if you still believe the real chance is higher than the current price. Sell if your reason for the trade has changed, if the gain is large, or if you need the money.

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: prices and the order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
2. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)
3. [MOONX Terms of Service, section 11: fees](/terms)

# Long shots on Polymarket: why 5¢ pays 20x, and why most never do

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/long-shot-trades
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: A long shot is a cheap share, usually under 10¢, that pays a big multiple if it wins: 20x at 5¢, 100x at 1¢. The market prices it as unlikely, and most long shots lose. Research on betting and prediction markets often finds long shots slightly overpriced, and fees take a bigger bite at low prices. Treat them as small, fun bets you can afford to lose, and consider selling early if the price jumps.

## The appeal, in one table

| Price | Multiple if it wins | $5 becomes | Market's estimate |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1¢ | 100x | $500 | 1 in 100 |
| 2¢ | 50x | $250 | 1 in 50 |
| 5¢ | 20x | $100 | 1 in 20 |
| 10¢ | 10x | $50 | 1 in 10 |

Before fees. If the prices are fair, buying twenty different 5¢ shares should produce about one winner. One winner at 20x pays for the nineteen losers, and you end up roughly where you started. That's what "fair odds" means.

## Are long shots fairly priced?

Not always, and the error tends to go one way. Economists have studied the **favourite-longshot bias** for decades: in horse racing and many betting markets, long shots win less often than their prices suggest, and favourites a bit more often. [Wolfers and Zitzewitz (2004)](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/0895330041371321) discuss it in their review of prediction markets.

The usual explanations are human. People enjoy the dream of a 50x, so they pay a little too much for it. And at very low prices, a cent is a huge share of the price, so small mistakes in pricing become big ones.

Practically: a 3¢ share is not a 3% chance just because the screen says so. It may be less.

## Fees hit hardest at low prices

On Polymarket, the taker fee as a share of your stake is the category rate times (1 − price). Near zero, that is almost the full rate: about **6.65% at 5¢ on a crypto market**, against 3.5% at 50¢. The spread matters too: buying at 6¢ instead of 5¢ cuts your multiple from 20x to 16.7x. Details in [Polymarket fees](/learn/polymarket-fees).

## The part people forget: you can sell before the end

Long shots don't have to go all the way to win you money. A share bought at 3¢ that rises to 15¢ on news is **5x** already. You can take it then, even if the event never happens. Many of the best long-shot trades end this way, with a sale, not a resolution. See [selling before the result](/learn/sell-before-the-result).

::: ex Worked example
You put **$5** on a 4¢ share: 125 shares. A surprise result in the semi-final pushes it to **18¢**. Selling at 17¢ brings in about $21 before fees: more than 4x, without waiting for the final. If you had held and the team lost the final, the shares would be worth nothing.
:::

## A sane way to play moonshots

- **Small amounts only.** Size each long shot so that losing it changes nothing for you. Expect to lose most of them.
- **Spread, don't stack.** Ten $2 long shots on unrelated events behave very differently from one $20 bet.
- **Read the rules.** Long shots often win on technicalities, and lose on them too. Check exactly what counts as Yes.
- **Have an exit price in mind.** Decide in advance at what price you'd take a gain.
- **Check the volume.** On a quiet market you may not find a buyer at a good price when you want out.

## What a real long shot looks like

When MOONX launched its $500 challenge in October 2026, the best trade on the MOONX leaderboard was a **27x** on a Bitcoin call, held until the market resolved. It happens. It's also exactly why it's on a leaderboard: most trades at that price don't make it.

::: risk Before you chase a big number
Big multiples come from unlikely outcomes, and most unlikely outcomes don't happen. Only put in what you can afford to lose.
:::

## Common questions {faq}

### What is a long shot on Polymarket?

A share priced low, often under 10¢, because the market thinks the outcome is unlikely. It pays a large multiple if it wins: 1 divided by the price.

### Can you make money buying cheap Polymarket shares?

Sometimes, but not by default. If prices are fair, many small long shots roughly break even before fees. Research often finds long shots slightly overpriced, and fees are highest at low prices in percentage terms.

### What is the favourite-longshot bias?

A pattern found in many betting markets: unlikely outcomes win less often than their prices imply, and likely outcomes a little more often.

### Should I hold a long shot until the end?

Only if you still think the real chance is higher than the price. If the price has jumped, selling locks in the multiple without the risk of the last step.

## Sources {src}

1. [Wolfers, J. and Zitzewitz, E. (2004), Prediction Markets, Journal of Economic Perspectives](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/0895330041371321)
2. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)
3. [Polymarket documentation: prices and the order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)

# Prediction markets vs sports betting: what is actually different

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/prediction-markets-vs-sports-betting
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: With a bookmaker, the bookmaker sets the odds, builds in a margin and takes the other side of your bet. On a prediction market like Polymarket, you trade with other people at a price that moves, the platform earns a trading fee instead of a margin, and you can sell your position before the end. How the law treats each one depends on the country.

## Side by side

| | Bookmaker | Prediction market |
|---|---|---|
| Who sets the price | The bookmaker | Traders, through an order book |
| Who is on the other side | The bookmaker | Another trader |
| How the platform earns | A margin built into the odds | A trading fee, separate from the price |
| Can you exit early | Sometimes, through a cash-out offer set by the bookmaker | Yes, sell to another trader at any time |
| Price after you buy | Your odds are fixed | Your shares rise and fall with the market |
| Winners limited | Some bookmakers limit winning accounts | The market doesn't care who you are |
| What you can trade | Mostly sports | Sports, crypto, politics, news, culture |

## Odds versus prices

A bookmaker quotes odds like 2.50. A prediction market quotes a price like 40¢. They express the same thing: 1 ÷ 0.40 = 2.50. A 40¢ share that wins pays $1, which is 2.5 times your money. The table in [prediction market odds](/learn/prediction-market-odds) converts any price into decimal and American odds.

## Where the margin goes

Add up the implied probabilities of all outcomes in a bookmaker's market and you usually get more than 100%. The excess, often called the overround, is the bookmaker's margin. It's built into every price you see.

On a prediction market, Yes plus No add up to about $1, with a small spread between buying and selling prices. The platform's income is a separate trading fee. On Polymarket that fee depends on the category and the price, and it's zero on some markets (see [Polymarket fees](/learn/polymarket-fees)). Neither model is free. The difference is that a fee is visible, while a margin is hidden inside the odds.

## Selling before the end

This is the biggest practical difference. On a prediction market your position is an asset you can sell to another trader at the current price, whenever you want. If your team goes 2-0 up at half-time, the price of your Yes shares jumps, and you can take the gain then.

Many bookmakers offer a cash-out too, but the bookmaker sets that price, and it can be withdrawn at any time. On a market, the price comes from other traders.

## Who you're up against

A bookmaker profits when bettors lose, so it manages risk: it adjusts odds, and some limit customers who win too often. On a prediction market, the platform earns the same fee whoever wins. You are trading against other people, some of them very well informed. That cuts both ways: no one limits you for winning, but the price you're buying is often a sharp one.

## What about the law?

Rules differ a lot from one country to another. Some regulators treat prediction markets as financial contracts, others treat them as gambling, and some block them. Polymarket restricts access in a number of countries. Check what applies where you live before you trade.

## Which one suits you?

- If you want **fixed odds on a single game** and you're happy with a bookmaker's margin, a bookmaker does the job.
- If you want to **trade the price as things happen**, sell early, or bet on things beyond sports, a prediction market fits better.

## Common questions {faq}

### Is Polymarket a betting site?

Polymarket is a prediction market: traders buy and sell shares in outcomes with each other, and Polymarket doesn't set odds or take the other side. How a country classifies it legally is a separate question with different answers in different places.

### Are prediction market odds better than bookmaker odds?

Often they are close to fair, because there is no margin built into the price. But you also pay a trading fee and a spread, so compare the full cost on the specific market.

### Can I bet on sports on Polymarket?

Yes. Polymarket lists many sports markets, from single matches to league titles. On most of them, takers pay a fee at a rate of 0.05 under Polymarket's fee formula.

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: prices and the order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
2. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)
3. [Wolfers, J. and Zitzewitz, E. (2004), Prediction Markets, Journal of Economic Perspectives](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/0895330041371321)

# Multi-outcome markets on Polymarket: elections, awards and "Other"

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/multi-outcome-markets
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: A multi-outcome market on Polymarket is a group of Yes/No markets, one per possible answer, where only one can resolve Yes. The Yes prices across all answers add up to about $1. Buying No on one candidate is economically the same as betting on all the others, which Polymarket calls negative risk. If new names can be added later, avoid trading the placeholder "Other".

## One question, many small markets

Take "Who will win the Ballon d'Or?". Polymarket lists each candidate with its own price, say:

| Candidate | Yes price | Multiple if right |
|---|---:|---:|
| Player A | 52¢ | 1.9x |
| Player B | 27¢ | 3.7x |
| Player C | 12¢ | 8.3x |
| Player D | 9¢ | 11.1x |

These are illustrative numbers. Behind the scenes, each line is a separate Yes/No market: "Will Player A win?", "Will Player B win?", and so on. Exactly one of them will resolve Yes.

## Why the prices add up to about $1

Since only one candidate wins, holding one Yes share of every candidate guarantees exactly $1 at the end. So the Yes prices across the whole list should add up to about $1, give or take the spread. If they add up to much more or less, traders step in and the gap closes.

This is also a quick sanity check when you read a market: if the favourite is at 52¢, the others share about 48¢ between them.

## Buying No on one candidate

You can buy **No** on any line. "No on Player A" pays $1 if anyone other than Player A wins. Polymarket links these markets with a mechanism it calls **negative risk**: one No share on a candidate can be converted into one Yes share on every other candidate in the event, in a single transaction.

What it means for you: betting against one outcome is economically the same as betting on all the others, without having to buy each of them.

::: ex Worked example
You think Player A is overrated at 52¢. You buy No on Player A at about 48¢. If Player B, C or anyone else wins, each share pays **$1**: about 2.1x. If Player A wins, you lose your stake.
:::

## The "Other" trap

Some events start before every candidate is known, like a party's nominee a year before the primaries. Polymarket can add new names later, using placeholders. If the winner is never named in the list, the market resolves to **"Other"**, and what "Other" covers can change as placeholders are clarified.

Polymarket's own documentation advises trading only named outcomes and avoiding "Other" directly. Follow that advice.

## Tips for reading multi-outcome markets

- **Check the volume per line, not just the event.** A candidate at 3¢ may have very few buyers and sellers.
- **Read the rules once for the whole event.** They define what counts as winning for every line.
- **Watch for withdrawals.** If a candidate drops out, their line usually goes to almost zero and the others reprice within minutes.

## Common questions {faq}

### How do multiple-choice markets work on Polymarket?

Each possible answer is its own Yes/No market, and only one answer can resolve Yes. Yes on the winning answer pays $1, and Yes on every other answer pays nothing. No on any losing answer pays $1.

### What is negative risk on Polymarket?

A link between the markets of one event: a No share on one outcome can be converted into a Yes share on each of the other outcomes. It makes betting against one outcome the same as betting on all the others.

### Should I buy "Other"?

Polymarket's documentation advises against trading "Other" directly in events where new outcomes can be added, because what it covers can change.

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: negative risk markets](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/negative-risk)
2. [Polymarket documentation: resolution](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/resolution)


---

# Polymarket glossary: every word you will see, explained

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/polymarket-glossary
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: The words that matter most: a share pays $1 if its outcome is right. The price is between 0 and $1 and reads as a probability. The bid is the best price buyers offer, the ask is the best price sellers accept, and the spread is the gap. A taker fills against existing orders and pays Polymarket's fee. Resolution is when the result is confirmed, usually through the UMA oracle.

## A to M

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Ask** | The lowest price a seller currently accepts. Buying right away fills at the ask. |
| **Bid** | The highest price a buyer currently offers. Selling right away fills at the bid. |
| **Bond** | Money a proposer or disputer puts up during resolution, typically $750. They lose it if they're wrong. |
| **Builder** | An app that sends its users' orders to Polymarket and is credited for that volume. MOONX is one. |
| **Chainlink** | The price feed used to settle short crypto Up or Down markets automatically. |
| **Combo** | Several outcomes combined into one position, priced by market makers on request. |
| **Dispute** | A challenge to a proposed result, made by posting a bond within the challenge window. |
| **DVM** | UMA's Data Verification Mechanism: the vote by UMA token holders that settles a twice-disputed result. |
| **Eject** | MOONX's sell button. One tap sells your position at the best price on the book. |
| **Implied probability** | The chance a price represents. 30¢ means about 30%. |
| **Limit order** | An order with a price limit. It can wait in the book until someone takes it. |
| **Liquidity** | How much is available to buy and sell near the current price. More liquidity means smaller price moves when you trade. |
| **Maker** | A trader whose order waits in the book and is filled by someone else. Makers pay no fee on Polymarket. |
| **Market order** | An order that fills right away at the best available prices. |
| **Midpoint** | Halfway between the best bid and best ask. Polymarket shows it as the price when the spread is 10¢ or less. |
| **Multiple** | What a share pays relative to its price if it wins: 1 divided by the price. 20¢ is 5x. |

## N to Z

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Negative risk** | In a multi-outcome event, a No share on one outcome can be converted into a Yes share on each of the others. |
| **No share** | Pays $1 if the outcome does not happen. |
| **Order book** | The list of all open buy and sell orders on a market. |
| **Outcome** | One possible answer to a market's question. |
| **Polygon** | The blockchain Polymarket runs on. MOONX wallets live on it too. |
| **Position** | The shares you hold in a market. |
| **pUSD** | The dollar token Polymarket uses to settle trades, backed by USDC. |
| **Resolution** | The moment the result is confirmed and winning shares pay $1. |
| **Rules** | The written conditions of a market: what counts as Yes, which source decides, and the deadline. |
| **Share** | A unit of a position. Pays $1 if its outcome is right, $0 if not. |
| **Shot** | MOONX's word for a trade: one position you open on a market. |
| **Spread** | The gap between the best bid and the best ask. What you pay to trade instantly. |
| **Taker** | A trader whose order fills right away against waiting orders. Takers pay Polymarket's fee on most markets. |
| **Tick size** | The smallest price step a market accepts, often 1¢. |
| **UMA Optimistic Oracle** | The independent system that resolves most Polymarket markets through proposals, bonds and disputes. |
| **USDC** | A dollar stablecoin. MOONX's main wallet holds USDC on Polygon. |
| **Volume** | The total value traded on a market. Higher volume usually means tighter spreads. |
| **Yes share** | Pays $1 if the outcome happens. |

## Words MOONX uses

A few words are specific to MOONX. A **shot** is a trade. **Eject** sells it. Your **crew** is the people who joined through your invite link. The **feed** shows real trades from other MOONX users, and you can take the same side or the other one in a tap. More in [your first trade on MOONX](/learn/first-trade-on-moonx).

## Common questions {faq}

### What is the spread on Polymarket?

The difference between the best price buyers offer (bid) and the best price sellers accept (ask). On busy markets it is often a single tick.

### What is the difference between a maker and a taker?

A maker's order waits in the book. A taker's order fills right away against it. On Polymarket, takers pay a fee on most markets and makers pay none.

### What does resolution mean?

The point where a market's result is confirmed. Winning shares then pay $1 and losing shares $0.

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: prices and the order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
2. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)
3. [Polymarket documentation: resolution](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/resolution)
4. [Polymarket documentation: negative risk markets](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/negative-risk)
5. [Polymarket documentation: pUSD](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/pusd)

# Your first trade on MOONX, step by step

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/first-trade-on-moonx
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Sign up on MOONX with your email and explore the app. Then set up your wallet, which takes about two minutes: no seed phrase, one backup file and a password that only you keep, and a PIN of six to twelve digits. Add money with a card, or send USDC on Polygon. Then open a market, choose Yes or No and an amount, check the cost and confirm with your PIN. Sell anytime with Eject.

## Before you start

You need an email address, a phone or a computer, and a payment card or some USDC. You don't need a crypto wallet, a seed phrase, or any token to pay network fees: MOONX handles that part.

You must be 18, or the age of majority where you live if that's higher. MOONX is not available everywhere, including the US and the UK. The full list is in the [Terms](/terms).

## 1. Create your account

Go to [moonx.fi](/) and tap **Create account**. Enter your email and open the sign-in link MOONX sends you. There's no password to invent for logging in.

You can now explore the whole app: the feed, the markets, the prices.

## 2. Set up your wallet

To trade, you finish your onboarding and get your wallet. MOONX is invite-only for now: if the app asks for an access code, it shows you how to get one for free.

Your wallet is created **on your own device**, and only you can move the money in it. Setup takes about two minutes:

1. Give your account a name.
2. Your device creates your wallet.
3. Save **one backup file**: it's an encrypted copy of your wallet.
4. Choose **a password** for that file. Keep the file and the password somewhere safe: MOONX doesn't keep a copy, and losing either one means losing access for good.
5. Choose a **PIN** of six to twelve digits for this device. It approves every trade and every money move.

Why this matters, and how to use the same wallet on another device, is explained in [your MOONX wallet](/learn/moonx-wallet).

## 3. Add money

- **By card, mobile wallet or bank transfer:** like any online purchase. The payment is handled by MOONX's payment partners, Stripe and Swapped through Calm Treasury, and any fee they charge is shown before you pay.
- **With USDC:** if you already have some, send USDC on the **Polygon** network from another wallet or an exchange to your MOONX address. Sending on another network can lose the funds, so check the network twice.

Your money lands in your main wallet, in dollars (USDC).

## 4. Pick a market

Browse the **feed** of real trades from other MOONX traders, or search all of Polymarket: sports, crypto, politics, the news. Open a market and read its rules once: they say exactly what counts as Yes.

## 5. Choose Yes or No, and an amount

Each side shows its price, which is also the market's estimate of the odds. Enter your amount and MOONX shows how many shares you get and what they pay if you're right.

::: ex Worked example
Yes is at **20¢**. You enter **$10**. You get 50 shares, which pay **$50** if Yes wins: 5x your money, before fees. MOONX shows the full cost, fees included, before you confirm.
:::

Confirm with your PIN. Your wallet signs the order and MOONX passes it to Polymarket, moving the money for you. You don't pay network fees.

## 6. Follow it, then sell or wait

Your position updates as the price moves. You have two ways out:

- **Sell anytime with Eject.** One tap sells at the best price on the book. MOONX shows the price and the fee before you confirm. On a quiet market it can fill lower, or only partly. Useful to lock in a gain or limit a loss. See [selling before the result](/learn/sell-before-the-result).
- **Hold to the end.** When the market resolves, winning shares pay $1 each, and the money lands in your MOONX wallet, usually within a few minutes, sometimes a few hours. You don't need to do anything.

## 7. Withdraw

First add the address you want to send to, such as an exchange account or another wallet that accepts **USDC on Polygon**, to your **Payout Wallets** list (up to five). Then withdraw whenever you want. There is no withdrawal fee, and network fees are on MOONX. A withdrawal to a wrong address can't be reversed, so check it twice.

## What it costs

MOONX charges 1% of the trade value when you buy and when you sell. Polymarket's own fee applies on most markets, depending on the category and the price. Nothing is charged when a market resolves. Every fee is included in what you see before you confirm. All the numbers are in [Polymarket fees](/learn/polymarket-fees).

## Common questions {faq}

### Do I need crypto to use MOONX?

No. You can add money with a card, a mobile wallet or a bank transfer. If you already hold USDC, you can also send it on the Polygon network.

### How long does it take to start?

Signing up takes a minute and setting up the wallet about two more. Then you can add money and trade.

### What is the minimum to trade?

Trades start at just over $1. Above 20¢ a share, a 5-share minimum can make it more, for example $2.50 at 50¢. See [the minimum bet on Polymarket](/learn/polymarket-minimum-bet).

### Can I use MOONX on my phone and my computer?

Yes, with the same wallet. Log in with your email on the other device, upload your backup file and enter its password, then choose a PIN for that device.

## Sources {src}

1. [MOONX Terms of Service](/terms)
2. [MOONX Privacy Policy](/privacy)
3. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)

# Your MOONX wallet: who holds the keys, and what you must keep

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/moonx-wallet
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Your MOONX wallet is non-custodial: its keys are created on your device and MOONX never holds them, so MOONX can't move, freeze or spend your money. You keep one encrypted backup file and its password. Each device you use gets a PIN that approves every trade and money move. If you lose the backup file or its password, nobody can recover the wallet, MOONX included.

## Non-custodial, in one sentence

MOONX is software that helps your device create and use a wallet. It never holds your money or your keys. In the words of MOONX's Terms, it has no ability to move, freeze or access a single dollar in your wallet.

Compare that with an exchange account: there, the company holds the money and you hold a login. If the company fails or freezes accounts, your balance is stuck. With a non-custodial wallet, the money is under your keys, on a public blockchain.

## The three things you hold

| What | What it does | Who has it |
|---|---|---|
| **Backup file** | An encrypted copy of your wallet keys | You only. MOONX doesn't keep a copy. |
| **Backup password** | Unlocks the backup file | You only |
| **PIN** | Approves every trade and every money move on one device | You only, one per device |

You log in with your email. Logging in shows your account. It's the PIN that lets money move, and the backup file with its password that lets you bring your wallet to a new device. You can also add passkeys to secure your account.

::: risk The one thing you must not lose
If you lose the backup file **or** its password, the money in that wallet is lost for everyone: one doesn't work without the other. MOONX can't restore it, by design. Store the file somewhere you won't delete it, such as a cloud drive and a USB stick, and the password in a password manager.
:::

## Using MOONX on another phone or computer

1. Open MOONX on the new device and log in with your email.
2. Upload your backup file.
3. Enter its password. Your wallet, your money and your trades are all there.
4. Choose a PIN for this device, the same one or a new one.

## Where your money actually is

MOONX wallets live on the **Polygon** blockchain, the same network Polymarket runs on. Your wallet has up to three parts:

- **Main wallet:** your dollars, in USDC. Deposits arrive here and withdrawals leave from here.
- **Trading wallet:** the money in play on Polymarket, which settles in pUSD. MOONX moves money between the two when you trade.
- **Savings (optional):** unused cash can earn interest through Aave, a third-party lending protocol, at a variable rate. You can ask for it back at any time. Withdrawals depend on Aave having money available, so they can be delayed, and lending protocols carry their own risks.

MOONX pays the network fees for all of this, so you never need to hold another token.

Withdrawals can only go to addresses on your **Payout Wallets** list, up to five, that you set yourself. It's a safeguard that runs in your wallet, not a service MOONX operates. Check each address carefully, because a withdrawal to a wrong address can't be reversed.

## What MOONX can and can't do

| MOONX can | MOONX can't |
|---|---|
| Show you markets and prices | Move your money: only your device can, with your PIN |
| Pass the orders you confirm to Polymarket | Freeze or seize your wallet |
| Pay network fees for you | Recover a wallet if you lose the backup file or its password |
| Help you set up a new device with your backup | See your PIN or your backup password |

## Common questions {faq}

### Is MOONX custodial?

No. The wallet keys are generated on your device and never sent to MOONX. Only you can move your money.

### What happens if I lose my phone?

Log in on another device with your email, upload your backup file and enter its password. Your wallet comes back with your money and your trades. Then choose a new PIN.

### Can MOONX recover my wallet if I lose my backup file?

No. MOONX keeps no copy of your backup file or your password. Without both, nobody can restore the wallet.

### Is there a seed phrase?

No. MOONX uses one encrypted backup file and a password instead of a list of words to write down.

## Sources {src}

1. [MOONX Terms of Service, section 5: your wallet and self-custody](/terms)
2. [MOONX Privacy Policy](/privacy)
3. [Aave](https://aave.com)

# Earn with MOONX: your crew and trades taken from your posts

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/earn-with-moonx
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: You earn in two ways on MOONX. Your crew: everyone who joins with your invite link earns you 25% of MOONX's fee on all their trades, for life. Your posts: when someone trades a market from one of your trades, on either side, you earn 25% of MOONX's fee on that trade and their later trades on that market. Both can add up to 50%. It's paid in USDC around the 1st of each month.

## Where the money comes from

MOONX earns a fee of 1% of the trade value when someone buys or sells. Part of that fee goes to you. It comes out of MOONX's share, never out of the trader's: your friends pay exactly the same fees as anyone else.

You earn on **trading**, not on results. You earn the same whether the other person wins or loses.

## 1. Your crew: 25% for life

Share your invite link. Everyone who opens their account through it joins your **crew**. You then earn **25% of MOONX's fee on all their trades**, buys and sells, for as long as their account runs. No cap.

::: ex Worked example
A friend in your crew trades **$1,000** in a month. MOONX's fee is 1%, so $10. You earn **$2.50**. Ten friends who each trade $1,000 a month: **$25** a month.
:::

## 2. Your posts: 25% when people trade from you

Your trades can appear in the MOONX feed, on your profile, or on a card you share. When another user **trades a market from one of them**, you earn **25% of MOONX's fee** on that trade. It works whichever side they take, the same as you or the opposite.

It doesn't stop there: you also earn on **their later trades on that market**, until it settles, or until they trade that market from someone else's post.

- Only opening your post earns nothing. They have to trade from it.
- It doesn't matter whether they had already traded that market before.
- Your own trades never earn you this reward.

## Both add up

If someone in your crew trades from your post, you earn both: **50% of MOONX's fee** on that trade. If your crew member trades from someone else's post, you keep your 25% and the author of the post earns theirs.

| Who trades | From whose post | You earn |
|---|---|---|
| Your crew member | Nobody's | 25% of our fee |
| Anyone | Yours | 25% of our fee |
| Your crew member | Yours | 50% of our fee |
| Your crew member | Someone else's | 25% (they earn 25% too) |

## When you get paid

Earnings build up over each calendar month and are paid together in **USDC**, into your main wallet, on or around the **1st of the following month**. A month under $5 in total isn't paid out: it rolls into the next month.

## The rules that keep it fair

Fake accounts, referring yourself, trading from your own posts through another account, groups of accounts trading from each other's posts, and bought or incentivised traffic earn nothing, and the earnings can be reversed. When you share, don't promise returns, don't present MOONX as an investment, and don't send it to people in countries where MOONX isn't available. Earnings are yours once they are paid, MOONX can change, pause or end the programme with notice, and taxes on what you earn are your responsibility. The full rules are in sections 10 and 12 of the [Terms](/terms).

## Common questions {faq}

### How much do I earn when a friend joins MOONX?

25% of MOONX's fee on every trade they make, buys and sells, for as long as their account runs. MOONX's fee is 1% of the trade value, so that's 0.25% of what they trade.

### Does my friend pay more because I invited them?

No. Your earnings come out of MOONX's share of the fee. Your friend pays exactly the same fees as any other user.

### Do I earn if someone takes the opposite side of my trade?

Yes. You earn the same reward whichever side they choose.

### When are referral earnings paid?

Monthly, in USDC, into your main wallet, around the 1st of the following month. Months under $5 roll over.

## Sources {src}

1. [MOONX Terms of Service, section 12: referrals and Shot rewards](/terms)
2. [MOONX Terms of Service, section 11: fees](/terms)

# Polymarket copy trading: follow a trade, or take the other side

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/polymarket-copy-trading
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Yes, you can follow Polymarket traders, because every trade is recorded on a public blockchain. But you will rarely get their price: by the time you see a trade, the market has often moved. Check the price you would pay, the size of their position, the market's volume and whether they are still in. On MOONX, the feed shows real trades from other users live, and you can take the same side or the opposite one in a tap.

## Why you can see other people's trades

Polymarket runs on the Polygon blockchain. Every position and every trade is recorded publicly, which is why each Polymarket account has a public profile with its positions and results. It's also why apps can build feeds, leaderboards and alerts around what traders do.

## Copying is not getting the same trade

Following a trader sounds simple: they buy, you buy. In practice, three things differ.

1. **Your price.** If a well-known trader buys Yes at 30¢, others follow and the price climbs. You might pay 36¢. Their 3.3x becomes your 2.8x.
2. **Your exit.** They may sell the next day, quietly. If you don't see it, you're holding a position its original owner has already left.
3. **Their size.** A $50,000 position can be a small hedge inside a big book. Your $20 copy of it is a full bet.

::: ex Worked example
A trader buys Yes at **25¢**. You see it an hour later and buy at **31¢**. The market resolves Yes: they make 4x, you make about 3.2x before fees. Now suppose they sold at 45¢ after a news spike and the market then resolved No: they made 1.8x, and you lost your stake.
:::

## What to check before you follow a trade

- **The price now, not their price.** Would you buy at today's price if nobody had bought before you?
- **Their record over many trades.** One huge win says little. A long history across different markets says more.
- **Whether they're still in.** Look at their current position, not just the entry.
- **The market's volume.** On a thin market, followers can push the price up just by arriving.
- **The rules of the market.** You are betting on the written rules, not on the trader's opinion.

## Taking the other side

Following works in both directions. If a trader you think is reckless piles into a long shot, the opposite side may be the better trade. Since Yes and No always add up to about $1, taking the other side is a full trade in its own right, with its own price and payout.

## How the MOONX feed works

MOONX shows a feed of real trades from MOONX users. Open one and choose: **the same side, or the other one**, and your amount. It's a normal trade, at today's price, which you confirm yourself with your PIN. MOONX never trades for you.

The person whose trade you opened earns a share of MOONX's fee on your trade, out of MOONX's share, not yours. You pay the same fees as anyone else. Your own trades can appear in the feed too, and you earn the same way when others trade from them. Details in [earn with MOONX](/learn/earn-with-moonx).

::: note Information, not advice
A trade in the feed shows what someone did, not what you should do. Treat it as an idea to check, and decide for yourself.
:::

## Common questions {faq}

### Can you copy trade on Polymarket?

You can follow other traders because all trades are public. There's no guarantee you'll get the same price, and you need to watch when they sell. Some apps, like MOONX, let you open someone's trade and take the same side or the opposite one in a tap.

### Can I see what other Polymarket traders are buying?

Yes. Polymarket profiles show positions and activity, and every trade is recorded on the Polygon blockchain.

### Is copying the best traders a good strategy?

It can surface good ideas, but you will usually enter later and at a worse price, and you may miss their exit. Judge the trade at the price you would pay.

### Do I pay more when I trade from someone's post on MOONX?

No. The reward for the author comes out of MOONX's fee share. You pay the same fees as any other trade.

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: prices and the order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
2. [MOONX Terms of Service, section 12: referrals and Shot rewards](/terms)

# What is MOONX? The social app to trade on Polymarket

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-is-moonx
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: MOONX (moonx.fi) is a consumer app built on Polymarket, one of the largest prediction markets. You sign up with an email, add money by card or with USDC, and buy Yes or No on sports, crypto, politics and the news in a few taps. A feed shows real trades from other users. The wallet is non-custodial, MOONX pays the network fees, and it charges 1% per trade.

## What you can do on MOONX

- **Trade every Polymarket market.** Sports, crypto, politics, the news, culture. Each question has a Yes and a No, priced between 0 and $1, and each winning share pays $1.
- **Follow the feed.** Scroll a feed of real trades from other MOONX users. Open one and take the same side, or the other one.
- **Sell whenever you want.** The Eject button sells your position before the end, at the best price on the book. See [selling before the result](/learn/sell-before-the-result).
- **Earn from your trades and your friends.** When people trade from your posts, or friends join with your link, you get part of MOONX's fee. See [earn with MOONX](/learn/earn-with-moonx).

## How MOONX differs from using Polymarket directly

The markets, prices and results are Polymarket's. MOONX is a Polymarket builder: an app that sends your orders to Polymarket. What changes is everything around the trade.

| | On MOONX |
|---|---|
| Sign-up | An email and about two minutes. No seed phrase, no ID document to sign up |
| Adding money | Card, mobile wallet or bank transfer through payment partners, or USDC on Polygon |
| Your wallet | Created on your device. Only you can move your money |
| Network fees | Paid by MOONX on every trade, sale and withdrawal |
| Social | A feed of real trades, and rewards when others trade from yours |
| Where | In a browser on your phone or computer (moonx.fi), or inside Telegram |

## What it costs

MOONX charges **1% of the trade value** when you buy and when you sell. Nothing when a market resolves, no subscription, no account fee, no withdrawal fee. Polymarket's own fee applies on most markets, depending on the category and price, and every fee is included in what you see before you confirm. Details in [Polymarket fees](/learn/polymarket-fees).

::: ex Worked example
You put **$10** on Yes at **25¢** in a politics market: 40 shares. MOONX's fee is $0.10. Polymarket's fee is 40 × 0.04 × 0.25 × 0.75 = $0.30. If Yes wins, the 40 shares pay **$40**.
:::

## Your money stays yours

MOONX never holds your funds or your keys. Your wallet is created on your device, you keep one encrypted backup file and its password, and a PIN approves every move. MOONX can't move, freeze or recover your money, which is also why the backup file and its password matter so much. More in [your MOONX wallet](/learn/moonx-wallet).

## Who runs MOONX

MOONX is operated from Hong Kong SAR, as stated in its [Terms](/terms). It's a Polymarket builder, and it's listed on the Polymarket Tools Directory. You can reach the team at hello@moonx.fi or through [@moonxfi on X](https://x.com/moonxfi).

## Who can use it

You must be 18, or the age of majority where you live if that's higher. MOONX is not available everywhere: not in the US, the UK, mainland China or Hong Kong, nor anywhere Polymarket restricts access. The full list is in the [Terms](/terms).

::: risk Before you start
Trading on prediction markets is risky. Big multiples come from unlikely outcomes, and most unlikely outcomes don't happen. Only put in what you can afford to lose.
:::

## Common questions {faq}

### Is MOONX the same as Polymarket?

No. Polymarket runs the markets. MOONX is an app built on top of it: your trades go to Polymarket, and your winnings come back to your MOONX wallet.

### Is MOONX free?

Signing up is free. MOONX charges 1% of the trade value when you buy or sell, and pays the network fees for you.

### Does MOONX have an app?

MOONX works in a browser on your phone or computer: go to [moonx.fi](/), and the app itself is at [lfg.moonx.fi](https://lfg.moonx.fi). It also runs inside Telegram as a Mini App, at [t.me/moonx_app_bot](https://t.me/moonx_app_bot).

### How do I start?

Sign up with your email at moonx.fi and explore the app, then set up your wallet and add money. The steps are in [your first trade on MOONX](/learn/first-trade-on-moonx).

## Sources {src}

1. [MOONX Terms of Service](/terms)
2. [Polymarket documentation: Builders Program](https://docs.polymarket.com/programs/builders/overview)
3. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)

# Are prediction markets accurate?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/are-prediction-markets-accurate
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Often, but not perfectly. A 2004 review by economists Justin Wolfers and Eric Zitzewitz found market forecasts typically fairly accurate and better than most moderately sophisticated benchmarks. A study of the Iowa Electronic Markets found the market closer to the final result than the polls 74% of the time, across 964 polls from five US presidential elections. The main known weakness is that cheap long shots tend to win less often than their prices suggest.

## What the research says

- **Wolfers and Zitzewitz (2004).** Reviewing data from many prediction markets, they conclude that market forecasts "are typically fairly accurate" and "outperform most moderately sophisticated benchmarks".
- **Berg, Nelson and Rietz (2008).** They compared 964 national polls from the 1988 to 2004 US presidential elections with the Iowa Electronic Markets at the same dates. The market was closer to the final vote share **74% of the time**, and it did significantly better than the polls in every election when forecasting more than 100 days ahead.
- **Cardozo and Rivero-Wildemauwe (2026).** A working paper, not yet peer reviewed, on 588 million Polymarket trades. In aggregate, purchases below 10¢ lost **19.3¢ per dollar**, while purchases at 90¢ or more earned **0.83¢ per dollar**. That's the favourite-longshot bias: long shots overpriced, favourites slightly underpriced. The pattern held in crypto and politics, not in sports. And it depends on how you count: weighting each contract equally, long shots lost 6.3¢ per dollar, but grouping related contracts by event, they gained 4.1¢.

## What "accurate" means for a price

A market price is a probability, not a yes-or-no call. So a market can be accurate and still "miss" often. The real test is calibration: of all the things priced at 70%, about 70% should happen.

::: ex Worked example
Take **100 markets**, each with Yes at **70¢**. You buy one Yes share in each: $70 in total.

- If prices are well calibrated, about 70 of them happen. You get **$70** back and break even, before fees.
- If only 60 happen, you get **$60** and lose $10. The market was overconfident.
- If 80 happen, you get **$80**. The market was too cautious.

Even in the calibrated case, 30 of the 100 "likely" outcomes don't happen. That's not the market being wrong.
:::

## Polymarket's own numbers

Polymarket publishes an accuracy page. When we checked it on 27 October 2026, it said the outcome leading **one month** before the end went on to win about **90%** of the time, and **98.7%** of the time **four hours** before. Two cautions: these are Polymarket's own figures, not an independent study, and the same page shows 78.3% of resolved markets ending No, so many markets are lopsided and a high hit rate is partly expected.

## Where markets get it wrong

- **Long shots.** Cheap shares tend to be overpriced, as above. See [long shots on Polymarket](/learn/long-shot-trades).
- **The rules.** A market resolves on its written rules, which can differ from what most people expect. See [what happens if a market is unclear](/learn/what-happens-if-a-polymarket-market-is-unclear).
- **Design.** Wolfers and Zitzewitz devote part of their review to market design, and note that carefully designed contracts can reveal the market's expectations through its prices.

For how prices work in the first place, read [what a prediction market is](/learn/what-is-a-prediction-market).

## Sources {src}

1. [Wolfers, J. and Zitzewitz, E. (2004), Prediction Markets, Journal of Economic Perspectives 18(2)](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/0895330041371321)
2. [Berg, J., Nelson, F. and Rietz, T. (2008), Prediction market accuracy in the long run, International Journal of Forecasting 24(2)](https://iemweb.biz.uiowa.edu/about-iem/research/prediction-market-accuracy-in-the-long-run/)
3. [Cardozo, M. and Rivero-Wildemauwe, J. I. (2026), The Favorite-Longshot Bias in Prediction Markets: Evidence from Polymarket, arXiv working paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12878)
4. [Polymarket accuracy page](https://polymarket.com/accuracy)
