# Can you use MOONX on your phone?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/can-i-use-moonx-on-my-phone
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Yes. MOONX works in your phone's browser: go to moonx.fi, and the app itself is at lfg.moonx.fi. It also runs inside Telegram as a Mini App. You can use the same wallet on your phone and your computer: log in with your email, upload your backup file, enter its password, and choose a PIN for that device.

## Where MOONX runs

| Where | How |
|---|---|
| Phone browser | Open [moonx.fi](/). The app itself is at [lfg.moonx.fi](https://lfg.moonx.fi). |
| Telegram | Open the MOONX Mini App at [t.me/moonx_app_bot](https://t.me/moonx_app_bot). |
| Computer | Same site, in any browser, with more room. |

## The same wallet on your phone and your computer

Your wallet is created on the first device you set it up on. To use it on another phone or computer:

1. Open MOONX there and log in with your email.
2. Upload your backup file.
3. Enter its password. Your money and your trades are all there.
4. Choose a PIN for this device, the same one or a new one.

It's one wallet on the Polygon blockchain, not one account per device.

::: ex Worked example
You set up MOONX on your phone and hold **$40** plus **2 open shots**. At home you open moonx.fi on your laptop, log in with your email, upload your backup file and type its password. The laptop shows the same **$40** and the same **2 shots**. You pick a PIN for the laptop. A trade you make there shows up on your phone too, because both devices use the same wallet.
:::

## Keeping your phone safe

- **The PIN protects each device.** It's 6 to 12 digits and approves every trade and every money move, so a phone left on a table isn't a wallet left open.
- **Lost your phone?** Log in on another device with your email, upload your backup file, enter its password, and choose a new PIN. Your wallet comes back with everything in it.
- **Don't keep your backup file only on your phone.** If the phone and the file disappear together, so does the wallet. Save the file in two places on the day you make it. See [what happens if you lose your backup file](/learn/what-if-i-lose-my-moonx-backup-file).

MOONX will never ask for your PIN, your backup password or your backup file, by email, in chat, on Telegram or in the app.

How the wallet, the backup and the PIN fit together is explained in [your MOONX wallet](/learn/moonx-wallet).

# Can you lose more than you bet on Polymarket?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/can-you-lose-more-than-you-bet-on-polymarket
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: No. When you buy a share on Polymarket you pay its full price up front, and a losing share is worth $0, never less. So the most you can lose on one trade is what you paid plus the trading fees, for example $10.66 on a $10 trade at 20¢ on a crypto market through MOONX. A losing trade can't leave you owing money.

## Why the loss stops at what you paid

Every Polymarket share is worth **$1** if its outcome happens and **$0** if it doesn't. Prices move between 0 and $1. You pay the price in full when you buy, so there's nothing left to pay later.

Betting against something works the same way. You don't borrow anything: you buy **No**, which also has a price you pay up front. If No loses, those shares go to $0, and that's the end of it.

::: ex Worked example
You put **$10** on Yes at **20¢** on a crypto market through MOONX. That's 10 ÷ 0.20 = **50 shares**.

- Polymarket's taker fee: 50 × 0.07 × 0.20 × 0.80 = **$0.56**
- MOONX's fee: 1% of $10 = **$0.10**
- Total cost: **$10.66**

If Yes loses, you lose $10.66. If Yes wins, you receive 50 × $1 = $50, a profit of $50 − $10.66 = **$39.34**. Nothing in between can cost you more than $10.66.
:::

## Fees are part of the loss

Fees are paid when your order is matched, not at the end. On most Polymarket markets the taker fee is shares × rate × price × (1 − price), with rates from 0.04 to 0.07 depending on the category, and 0 on geopolitics. MOONX adds 1% of the trade value when you buy and when you sell. There is no fee when a market resolves. So a full loss is your stake plus the fees you already paid. Details in [Polymarket fees](/learn/polymarket-fees).

## Selling at a loss

You can sell before the end. If you bought at 20¢ and the price drops to 8¢, selling 50 shares brings back about 50 × 0.08 = $4 before fees. You lose less than if you held to $0. A sale can bring back less than you hoped, but never a negative amount. See [selling before the result](/learn/sell-before-the-result).

## Where you can lose more than one bet

The cap applies trade by trade. Your total risk is bigger than that in a few cases:

- **Many trades.** Ten $10 trades can each go to $0. That's $100 plus fees at risk, not $10.
- **Your wallet.** MOONX is non-custodial. If you lose your backup file or its password, the whole wallet is lost for good, not just one bet. Read [what a non-custodial wallet is](/learn/what-is-a-non-custodial-wallet).
- **Outside risks.** MOONX's Terms list smart-contract failures and USDC losing its peg as risks, and there is no deposit insurance.

::: risk Said plainly
MOONX's Terms put it this way: prediction markets can lose you every dollar you put into a trade. Only put in what you can afford to lose entirely.
:::

For how a price turns into a payout, read [prediction market odds](/learn/prediction-market-odds).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: prices and the order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
2. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)
3. [MOONX Terms of Service, sections 5, 7 and 11](/terms)

# Can you use Polymarket with a credit or debit card?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/can-you-use-polymarket-with-a-card
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Polymarket itself settles every trade in pUSD, a dollar token on Polygon, and its help center and developer docs describe deposits as crypto transfers from supported networks. MOONX, an app built on Polymarket, lets you add money by card, mobile wallet or bank transfer through its payment partners, Stripe and Swapped, via Calm Treasury. The partner's fee is shown before you pay, and the money arrives as USDC in your own wallet.

## What Polymarket's own guides describe

Polymarket's help article on deposits and its developer documentation both describe the same method: **sending crypto to a deposit address**.

- You get a deposit address for each type of network: Ethereum and other EVM chains, Solana, Bitcoin and Tron.
- What you send is bridged and converted to **pUSD**, the dollar token used for all trading ([what is pUSD?](/learn/what-is-pusd)).
- Each asset has a minimum. The help center gives **$20 from Ethereum** and **$3 from Solana**. Smaller deposits stay pending until the total reaches the minimum.
- Polymarket charges **no fee to deposit or withdraw**. The service you use to move the money may charge its own.

These pages don't describe a card option. Polymarket's own app may show other ways to pay, so check it directly if you use it.

## Paying by card on MOONX

MOONX is an app built on Polymarket. You can add money in three ways besides sending crypto:

| Method | How it works |
|---|---|
| **Card** | Pay by card through a payment partner |
| **Mobile wallet** | Pay with the wallet on your phone |
| **Bank transfer** | Send money from your bank account |

Payments go through **Stripe and Swapped, via Calm Treasury**. Their fee is shown before you pay, so you see what you will receive before you confirm. The money arrives as **USDC on Polygon** in your MOONX wallet, which only you control. When you trade, MOONX moves it to Polymarket as pUSD and pays the network fees.

::: ex Worked example
You add **$50** by card and want to buy Yes at **40¢**.

1. The partner's screen shows its fee and the USDC you will get. Say it shows **49 USDC**. You confirm.
2. You buy Yes with **$20**. Before fees, that is 20 ÷ 0.40 = **50 shares**.
3. MOONX's fee is 1% of the trade: 1% of $20 is **$0.20**. Every fee is included in what you see before you confirm.
4. You still have about 49 − 20 = **29 USDC** in your wallet.

If Yes wins, the 50 shares pay **$50**. If No wins, they pay nothing.
:::

## Things to know before paying

- **The partner fee is separate** from MOONX's 1% trading fee and Polymarket's taker fee ([MOONX fees](/learn/moonx-fees)).
- **Payment partners may run their own identity checks** before they accept your payment.
- **Withdrawals don't go back to the card.** On MOONX, money leaves only to addresses on your Payout Wallets list, as USDC on Polygon ([how to withdraw from MOONX](/learn/how-to-withdraw-from-moonx)).
- **Availability varies.** Polymarket restricts some countries, and MOONX is not available everywhere (including the US, the UK, mainland China and Hong Kong; see the Terms). Check the rules where you live.

For the whole path from sign-up to your first position, read [your first trade on MOONX](/learn/first-trade-on-moonx).

2. [Polymarket documentation: deposit](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/bridge/deposit)
3. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)

# Do you need crypto to use Polymarket?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/do-you-need-crypto-to-use-polymarket
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: To trade on Polymarket, your money has to be in pUSD, Polymarket's dollar token on the Polygon blockchain, backed by USDC. You don't need to own bitcoin or any coin whose price moves, because pUSD is a dollar token. Polymarket's own deposit guides describe sending crypto from another wallet, but apps built on Polymarket, such as MOONX, let you pay by card, mobile wallet or bank transfer and convert the money for you.

## What Polymarket actually requires

Every trade on Polymarket is paid for in **pUSD**, a token on the Polygon blockchain backed by USDC, a dollar stablecoin ([what is pUSD?](/learn/what-is-pusd)). A winning share pays 1 pUSD. So, strictly speaking, yes: the money you trade with is a crypto token.

But it is a **dollar token**, not a coin with a moving price. Polymarket's documentation says pUSD's backing is enforced by a smart contract, with no algorithmic peg and no fractional reserve. You are betting on events, not on the price of a cryptocurrency, unless you choose a crypto market.

## Two ways to get there

**Send crypto you already have.** Polymarket's help center and developer docs describe deposits as crypto transfers: you get a deposit address and send tokens from a supported network (Ethereum and other EVM chains, Solana, Bitcoin, Tron). They are converted to pUSD automatically. This route assumes you already hold crypto somewhere and know which network to use.

**Pay with ordinary money through an app.** Some apps built on Polymarket handle the conversion. On **MOONX**, you can add money by **card, mobile wallet or bank transfer** through payment partners (Stripe and Swapped, via Calm Treasury). The partner's fee is shown before you pay, and payment partners may run their own identity checks. The money arrives as USDC in your MOONX wallet and moves to Polymarket as pUSD when you trade.

::: ex Worked example
You have never owned crypto. You want to put **$30** on a market.

1. In MOONX, choose to add money and pay **$30 by card**.
2. The partner's screen shows its fee and how much USDC you will receive. You confirm.
3. The USDC lands in your MOONX wallet on Polygon.
4. You buy Yes at **60¢** with $20. Before fees, that is 20 ÷ 0.60 ≈ **33.3 shares**. MOONX moves the $20 to Polymarket as pUSD for you.

At no point did you open a crypto exchange account, pick a network or buy a gas token. MOONX pays the network fees.
:::

## What you still take on

Not needing to buy crypto doesn't make the money less on-chain. A few things stay true:

- **Your wallet is yours to keep.** MOONX is non-custodial: you hold one backup file and its password. Lose either one and the money is gone for good ([what is a non-custodial wallet?](/learn/what-is-a-non-custodial-wallet)).
- **Withdrawals are blockchain transfers.** On MOONX they go only to addresses on your Payout Wallets list, and a transfer to a wrong address can't be reversed.
- **Availability depends on where you live.** Polymarket restricts some countries, and MOONX is not available everywhere (including the US, the UK, mainland China and Hong Kong; see the Terms). Check the rules where you live.

For the full setup, step by step, read [your first trade on MOONX](/learn/first-trade-on-moonx).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: Polymarket USD (pUSD)](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/pusd)
2. [Polymarket documentation: deposit](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/bridge/deposit)
3. [Polymarket Help Center: how to deposit](https://help.polymarket.com/en/articles/13369887-how-to-deposit)
4. [MOONX Terms of Service](/terms)

# Do you pay taxes on Polymarket winnings?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/do-you-pay-taxes-on-polymarket-winnings
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: It depends on the country where you live and pay tax, and on how it treats prediction market trading. MOONX gives no tax advice and doesn't withhold, collect or report tax for you, so working it out is your responsibility. Keep a record of every deposit, trade, sale, payout and withdrawal, with dates and amounts, and check with your tax authority or a qualified adviser.

## Why there's no single answer

Tax rules are set country by country. Depending on where you live, gains from prediction markets could fall under different headings, and the rules for each, including how losses and fees are handled, can differ. This page doesn't give country-specific answers. Your national tax authority's website, or a tax adviser who knows your situation, is the place to check.

## What MOONX does and doesn't do

MOONX's Terms are direct about it: you are responsible for determining, reporting and paying any taxes arising from your activity, including on **winnings, yield, referral earnings and shot rewards**. MOONX does not provide tax advice and does not withhold, collect or report taxes on your behalf.

So nothing is deducted from your winnings, and no tax form is sent anywhere for you.

## What to keep

Good records make any tax question easier. For each trade, note:

- **Date** of the buy and of the sale or payout
- **Market** and side (Yes or No)
- **Shares, price and amount** paid or received
- **Fees** paid, both Polymarket's and MOONX's
- **Deposits and withdrawals**, with dates and amounts
- Any **yield or referral earnings** received

Amounts on MOONX are in USDC, a dollar stablecoin. If your country taxes in another currency, also note the exchange rate on each date, in case you need it.

Your trades also leave a trail you can check later. MOONX's wallet is non-custodial and its activity settles on the Polygon blockchain, where transactions are public and linked to your wallet address.

::: ex Worked example: recording one trade
You buy **50 shares** of Yes at **20¢** on a crypto market: $10, plus a Polymarket fee of 50 × 0.07 × 0.20 × 0.80 = $0.56 and a MOONX fee of $0.10. **Total paid: $10.66.**

Later you sell all 50 at **60¢**: $30, minus a Polymarket fee of 50 × 0.07 × 0.60 × 0.40 = $0.84 and a MOONX fee of $0.30. **Total received: $28.86.**

The difference is $28.86 − $10.66 = **$18.20**. Whether that's the figure your country uses, and whether fees count, is for your local rules to say. Record losing trades the same way.
:::

::: note Not tax advice
This page explains what to record. It doesn't tell you what you owe. Check the rules where you live.
:::

For how money moves in and out of your wallet, read [the MOONX wallet guide](/learn/moonx-wallet).

2. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)
3. [Polymarket documentation: pUSD](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/pusd)

# How do Polymarket sports markets work?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/how-do-polymarket-sports-markets-work
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: A Polymarket sports market asks a question about a game or season, such as whether a team wins a match. You buy Yes or No shares from other traders at a price between 0 and $1, and each winning share pays $1 once the result is confirmed. The market's written rules say what counts and which source decides. Sports markets carry a taker fee rate of 0.05, about 2.5% of your stake at 50¢, and open limit orders are cancelled automatically when the game starts.

## The basics

A sports market works like any other Polymarket market:

- The question is written as a Yes or No, for example whether a given team wins a given match.
- A Yes share pays **$1** if it happens, **$0** if not. A No share is the reverse.
- The price reads as a probability. A team at 62¢ is seen as about a 62% chance.
- You buy from and sell to other traders through an order book. Polymarket doesn't set the odds or take the other side.

When a question has several possible answers, such as who wins a league, it is grouped into a multi-outcome event where only one answer can win. See [multi-outcome markets](/learn/multi-outcome-markets).

## The rules decide, not the title

Polymarket's documentation is clear: "The market title describes the question, but the rules define how it resolves." Each market's rules name the **resolution source**, the **end date** and how **ambiguous situations** are handled.

Before you trade a match, read the rules for the cases that catch people out. What happens on a draw, whether extra time counts, what happens if the game is postponed or cancelled. Don't assume: each market says it in writing. If something is unclear, see [what happens if a Polymarket market is unclear](/learn/what-happens-if-a-polymarket-market-is-unclear).

Sports results go through Polymarket's standard process, run by the UMA Optimistic Oracle: someone proposes the result, and if nobody disputes it within 2 hours, it stands. See [how long Polymarket takes to pay out](/learn/how-long-does-polymarket-take-to-pay-out).

## What happens at kickoff

According to Polymarket's documentation, open **limit orders** on sports markets are **cancelled automatically** once the game begins, clearing the book at the official start time. Start times can shift, and if a game starts earlier than scheduled, orders may not be cleared in time. If you leave orders in the book, watch them around the start.

## What it costs

::: ex Worked example
Team A is at **62¢** to win. You put in **$31** and get 31 ÷ 0.62 = **50 shares**.

Polymarket fee: 50 × 0.05 × 0.62 × 0.38 = about **$0.59**. On MOONX, add 1% of $31, about **$0.31**.

If Team A wins, you receive **$50**. Fees included, your profit is about 50 − 31 − 0.59 − 0.31 = **$18.10**.

If Team A doesn't win, the shares pay $0 and you lose your $31 plus fees.
:::

Sports markets carry a taker rate of **0.05**. As a share of what you spend, that's 0.05 × (1 − price): **2.5%** at 50¢, less on favourites, more on underdogs. There is no fee when the market resolves. Full table in [Polymarket fees](/learn/polymarket-fees).

You don't have to wait for the final whistle. You can sell your shares to another trader before the end, to lock in a gain or cut a loss. See [selling before the result](/learn/sell-before-the-result).

How this differs from a bookmaker is explained in [prediction markets vs sports betting](/learn/prediction-markets-vs-sports-betting).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: markets and events](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/markets-events)
2. [Polymarket documentation: resolution](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/resolution)
3. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)
4. [MOONX Terms of Service, section 11: fees](/terms)

# How do you make money on Polymarket?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/how-do-you-make-money-on-polymarket
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: There are two ways. Buy a share and hold it, and if your outcome wins, each share pays $1. Or sell it to another trader before the end for more than you paid, for example buying at 25¢ and selling at 50¢. Either way you profit only if you judged the chance better than the market did, and you can lose everything you put into a trade, plus fees.

## Way 1: be right at the end

Buy shares in an outcome and hold them until the market resolves. If it happens, each share pays **$1**. If not, they pay $0.

::: ex Worked example
You put **$10** on Yes at **25¢** on a sports market through MOONX: 10 ÷ 0.25 = **40 shares**.

- Polymarket fee: 40 × 0.05 × 0.25 × 0.75 = **$0.375**
- MOONX fee: 1% of $10 = **$0.10**
- Total cost: **$10.475**

Yes wins: you receive 40 × $1 = $40, a profit of about **$29.53**. Yes loses: you lose $10.475.
:::

## Way 2: sell higher before the end

You don't need to wait for the result. If the price rises after you buy, you can sell to another trader and keep the difference, even if the outcome never happens in the end.

::: ex Worked example
Same 40 shares bought at 25¢ for $10.475 in all. News pushes Yes to **50¢** and you sell.

- Sale: 40 × 0.50 = **$20**
- Polymarket fee: 40 × 0.05 × 0.50 × 0.50 = **$0.50**
- MOONX fee: 1% of $20 = **$0.20**

You keep $19.30, a profit of about **$8.83**, locked in whatever happens next.
:::

The same works in reverse: if the price falls, selling early limits the loss. More in [selling before the result](/learn/sell-before-the-result).

## The hard part

Both ways need the same thing: the price has to be wrong, and you have to be on the right side of the error. A share at 25¢ already means traders put the chance near 25%. If that's correct, buying it many times roughly breaks even before fees, and fees then push you below zero. You make money over time only if your estimates are better than the market's, which is hard. See [expected value](/learn/what-is-expected-value-in-prediction-markets).

Cheap shares are a special trap. Big multiples come from unlikely outcomes, and most unlikely outcomes don't happen. A 2026 working paper on 588 million Polymarket trades found that, in aggregate, purchases below 10¢ lost **19.3¢ per dollar**. The authors also show that the size of that loss depends on how trades are counted.

::: risk Before you start
There is no reliable way to profit on prediction markets. Put in only what you can afford to lose entirely.
:::

## Other ways people earn

Polymarket pays daily rewards to traders whose limit orders wait on the book close to the market price, on markets that have a reward set up, see [Polymarket rewards](/learn/what-are-polymarket-rewards). MOONX shares part of its own fee with people who bring in traders, see [earn with MOONX](/learn/earn-with-moonx). Neither needs you to predict anything, though resting orders carry their own risk.

For the price math behind every trade, read [prediction market odds](/learn/prediction-market-odds).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)
2. [Polymarket documentation: prices and the order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
3. [Cardozo and Rivero-Wildemauwe (2026), The Favorite-Longshot Bias in Prediction Markets: Evidence from Polymarket, arXiv working paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12878)
4. [MOONX Terms of Service, sections 7 and 11](/terms)

# How long does Polymarket take to pay out?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/how-long-does-polymarket-take-to-pay-out
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: After an event, someone proposes the result to Polymarket's oracle and a 2-hour challenge window opens. If nobody disputes it, the market resolves and each winning share is worth $1. A disputed result takes about 4 to 6 days in total. On MOONX, the money then lands in your wallet usually within minutes, sometimes a few hours.

## The timeline

Most Polymarket markets are resolved through the UMA Optimistic Oracle. The clock starts when someone **proposes** the result and posts a bond, typically $750.

| Stage | How long |
|---|---|
| Event ends, result proposed | Not fixed, depends on the market |
| Challenge window | 2 hours |
| Undisputed total, from the proposal | About 2 hours |
| Second dispute: debate, then UMA vote | 24 to 48 hours, then about 48 hours |
| Disputed total | About 4 to 6 days |

The first dispute throws out the proposal and starts a new round. Only a second dispute goes to a vote of UMA token holders. More on [UMA](/learn/what-is-uma-on-polymarket).

Short crypto **Up or Down** markets skip all of this. They settle automatically from a Chainlink price feed, with no proposal and no dispute. See [Up or Down markets](/learn/what-are-polymarket-up-or-down-markets).

::: ex Worked example
A match ends at 10 pm. Say someone proposes the result at 10:30 pm. Nobody disputes it, so it's final at about **12:30 am**. On MOONX, the money is usually in your wallet within minutes after that.

If the result were disputed twice, the same market could take about **4 to 6 days** to pay.
:::

## Selling instead of waiting

You don't have to wait for the payout. Once the result is obvious, the price usually climbs close to $1, and you can sell your shares to another trader. It costs you a little.

::: ex Worked example: selling at 99¢
You hold **100 shares** of the winning side on a sports market. The best bid is **99¢**.

- Sale: 100 × 0.99 = **$99**
- Polymarket fee: 100 × 0.05 × 0.99 × 0.01 = about **$0.05**
- MOONX fee: 1% of $99 = **$0.99**

You keep about **$97.96** now, against **$100** if you wait for resolution, where there is no fee.
:::

Whether $2.04 is worth paying for speed is your call. During a dispute, prices can swing again, so selling early also removes that risk. More in [selling before the result](/learn/sell-before-the-result).

## On MOONX

You don't need to claim anything. Once the market settles, the money lands in the wallet you traded from, usually within minutes, sometimes a few hours, as [your first trade on MOONX](/learn/first-trade-on-moonx) explains. There's no fee at resolution. From there you can trade again or withdraw to one of your saved payout wallets, see [how to withdraw from MOONX](/learn/how-to-withdraw-from-moonx).

MOONX doesn't decide results and can't speed up, change or reverse them. Resolution is handled by Polymarket's process.

For the full process, including bonds and votes, read [how Polymarket resolves markets](/learn/how-polymarket-resolves-markets).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: resolution](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/resolution)
2. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)
3. [MOONX guide: your first trade on MOONX](/learn/first-trade-on-moonx)

# How do you read a Polymarket chart?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/how-to-read-a-polymarket-chart
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: A Polymarket chart plots the price of a share over time. Because a winning share pays $1, a price of 30¢ reads as about a 30% chance, so the line shows how the market's implied probability has moved. A sudden jump usually means news or a large trade, a slow drift means opinion shifting, and as the deadline nears the line heads toward 0 or 100 as the answer becomes clear.

## The line is a probability

Every share on Polymarket pays **$1** if its outcome happens and **$0** if not. So its price, between 0 and $1, reads as a probability: 25¢ means the market puts the chance at about 25%. A chart of that price over time is a chart of how the market's view has changed.

Keep in mind how Polymarket sets the price it displays: it is the **midpoint** between the best bid and best ask, or the **last traded price** when the spread is wider than 10¢. On a quiet market, that number can rest on a single trade. More on what the number means in [what the percentage means on Polymarket](/learn/what-does-the-percentage-mean-on-polymarket).

## What the shapes mean

- **A sudden jump or drop.** Something happened: a result, a poll, an announcement, an injury. Traders reprice in minutes. On a quiet market, a single large order can also move the line without any news, by walking through the few orders in the book.
- **A slow drift.** Opinion is shifting gradually, as information builds up.
- **A flat line.** Either nothing has changed, or very few people are trading. A flat line on a thin market says less than a flat line on a busy one.
- **Spikes that snap back.** Often one trade on a thin book, not a real change in the odds.
- **A run to 0 or 100 near the end.** The answer is becoming known. Once the result is clear, the price settles near $1 or $0 before the market [resolves](/learn/how-polymarket-resolves-markets).

## Reading it as a trader

::: ex Worked example
A market's line sits at **22%** for weeks, then jumps to **61%** within an hour after an announcement.

Before the jump, a Yes share cost about 22¢ and would pay $1, about 1 ÷ 0.22 = **4.5x**. After it, a share costs about 61¢, about 1 ÷ 0.61 = **1.6x**.

Someone who bought at 22¢ and sells at 61¢ has multiplied their money by 61 ÷ 22 = about **2.8x**, before the spread and fees, without waiting for the result.
:::

Two questions to ask when you see a move:

1. **Is there a reason?** Look for the news behind it. A jump with no news on a thin market may not last.
2. **Is the market busy?** Check the [spread](/learn/what-is-the-spread-on-polymarket) and [volume](/learn/what-is-volume-on-polymarket). Busy markets move on information. Thin ones can move on a single order.

## Multi-outcome charts

When an event has several possible answers, such as who wins an election, each outcome has its own price and its own line. Only one can win, so the probabilities add up to roughly 100%. When one line rises, others usually fall. See [multi-outcome markets](/learn/multi-outcome-markets).

## What a chart doesn't tell you

The line is the crowd's current estimate, not a forecast you can count on. If a market at 80% is well calibrated, the 20% outcome still happens about one time in five. See [are prediction markets accurate](/learn/are-prediction-markets-accurate). How prices turn into odds and payouts is explained in full in [prediction market odds](/learn/prediction-market-odds).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: prices and the order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
2. [Polymarket documentation: negative risk markets](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/negative-risk)
3. [Polymarket documentation: resolution](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/resolution)

# How do you sell a position on MOONX?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/how-to-sell-on-moonx
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Tap Eject on your position. MOONX shows the price and the fee before you confirm, then sells your shares at the best price on the Polymarket order book once you confirm with your PIN, and the money goes back to your MOONX wallet. MOONX charges 1% of the sale value, and Polymarket's fee applies on most markets. On a thin or fast-moving market the price can be lower than shown, and a sale can fill partly, late or not at all.

## How Eject works

A sale needs a buyer. On Polymarket, buyers post the prices they're willing to pay in an order book. **Eject** sells your shares right away to the best of those offers, called the **bid**.

The price you see on a market is the midpoint between the best bid and the best ask (the cheapest seller). So a sale right now usually fills a little below the price shown. The gap between the two is the [spread](/learn/what-is-the-spread-on-polymarket). When the spread is wider than 10¢, Polymarket shows the last traded price instead.

MOONX shows the price and the fee before you confirm. You confirm with your PIN, like every trade.

::: ex Worked example
You hold **100 shares** of Yes, bought at 20¢ for $20, in a politics market (Polymarket rate 0.04). The best bid is **40¢** and the best ask 42¢, so the price shown is the midpoint, **41¢**. You tap Eject.

- Sale: 100 × 0.40 = **$40**
- MOONX fee: 1% of $40 = $0.40
- Polymarket fee: 100 × 0.04 × 0.40 × 0.60 = $0.96

You receive 40 − 0.40 − 0.96 = **$38.64**. The fees you paid when you bought are already behind you.
:::

## When the price is not what you tapped

On a quiet market, there may not be enough buyers at the best bid for all your shares. Say buyers at 40¢ only want 60 of your 100 shares: the other 40 may sell lower, or not right away. On a fast market, the bid can move between your tap and the fill. A sale can fill partly, late or not at all. Shares that don't sell stay in your position.

You'll find more on this in [what is slippage on Polymarket](/learn/what-is-slippage-on-polymarket) and [what is liquidity on Polymarket](/learn/what-is-liquidity-on-polymarket).

## Where the money goes

The money from the sale goes back to your **MOONX wallet**, in dollars. From there you can take another shot or withdraw it to an address on your Payout Wallets list, with no withdrawal fee. See [how to withdraw from MOONX](/learn/how-to-withdraw-from-moonx).

You can also just hold. When the market resolves, winning shares pay $1 each with no fee, and the money lands in your wallet, usually within minutes, sometimes a few hours.

When selling early makes sense, and when it doesn't, is covered in [selling before the result](/learn/sell-before-the-result).

## Sources {src}

1. [MOONX Terms of Service, sections 6 and 11](/terms)
2. [Polymarket documentation: prices and order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
3. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)

# How do you withdraw money from MOONX?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/how-to-withdraw-from-moonx
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Add the address you want to send to, such as an exchange account or another wallet that accepts USDC on Polygon, to your Payout Wallets list, which holds up to five addresses. Then withdraw from the app and confirm with your PIN. MOONX charges no withdrawal fee and pays the network fee. A withdrawal to a wrong address can't be reversed, so check it twice.

## Step by step

1. **Make sure the money is free to send.** You withdraw money that's available in your wallet, not money that's still in a trade or in savings. Money in a trade comes back when you sell it with Eject or when the market resolves. Money in savings has to come back from Aave first, which depends on Aave having money available.
2. **Find a receiving address that accepts USDC on Polygon.** On an exchange, that means choosing USDC and the Polygon network when you look up your deposit address.
3. **Add it to your Payout Wallets list.** Your wallet can only send withdrawals to addresses on this list, up to five. It's a safeguard that runs in your wallet, not a service MOONX operates.
4. **Withdraw.** Choose the address and the amount, then confirm with your PIN. Nothing leaves your wallet unless you choose and confirm it, and once it's sent, MOONX can't stop or reverse it.

## What it costs

MOONX charges **no withdrawal fee**, and it pays the network (gas) fee on the transfer, so you don't need any other token in your wallet. Polymarket charges nothing to withdraw either. The exchange or wallet that receives your USDC may charge its own fee, for example to convert it into your currency. Check its fees before you send.

::: ex Worked example
A market resolves your way and your **80 shares** pay 80 × $1 = **$80** into your main wallet. You already had **$15** there, so you hold 80 + 15 = **$95**. You withdraw all of it to your exchange's USDC on Polygon address, already on your Payout Wallets list. MOONX takes **$0** and pays the network fee. Your exchange receives **95 USDC**, minus any fee the exchange itself charges.
:::

::: risk Check the address, every time
A withdrawal sent to a wrong or compromised address can't be reversed, by MOONX or anyone else. Before you add an address to your Payout Wallets list, check it character by character, and check that it accepts **USDC on Polygon**. Sending to an address that doesn't can mean losing the money.
:::

## Leaving MOONX completely

You don't need MOONX to reach your money. Your wallet is non-custodial, and MOONX's Terms (section 20) state that your funds remain reachable with your Backup through any compatible wallet software. More on what that means in [what is a non-custodial wallet](/learn/what-is-a-non-custodial-wallet).

For the whole path from sign-up to withdrawal, read [your first trade on MOONX](/learn/first-trade-on-moonx).

## Sources {src}

1. [MOONX Terms of Service, sections 5, 11 and 20](/terms)
2. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)

# Is MOONX safe?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/is-moonx-safe
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: MOONX is non-custodial: your wallet keys are created on your device and MOONX never holds them, so it can't move, freeze or spend your money, and your funds stay on the Polygon blockchain even if MOONX shuts down. Your trades go to Polymarket, and MOONX is a Polymarket builder. What no app can protect you from: losing a trade, losing your backup file or its password, sending money to a wrong address, or a failure at Polymarket, Polygon or the USDC issuer.

## What MOONX can't do with your money

Your wallet is created on your own device, and its keys are generated and kept there. MOONX's Terms say it holds no copy of your keys, your backup file, your backup password or your PIN, and has no ability to move, freeze or access a single dollar in your wallet.

In practice:

- Nothing moves without your PIN, on your device. MOONX has no bot or agent trading for you.
- MOONX can't close a trade or stop a withdrawal. It can stop serving the app to a region or an account, and that's all: you still hold every dollar and every position.
- MOONX never takes the other side of your trades and makes nothing when you lose.

The same design has a hard edge: because MOONX can't reach your wallet, it can't recover it either. See [what happens if you lose your backup file](/learn/what-if-i-lose-my-moonx-backup-file).

## Where your money and trades actually are

Your main wallet holds USDC on **Polygon**, a public blockchain. When you trade, your wallet signs the order and MOONX passes it to Polymarket, which places, matches and settles it under its own rules. Polymarket runs on Polygon too.

MOONX is a **Polymarket builder**. Polymarket's Builders Program is how apps send their users' orders to Polymarket with a builder code, and builder volume is public on builders.polymarket.com. It tells you where your orders go. It isn't insurance. More in [what is a Polymarket builder](/learn/what-is-a-polymarket-builder).

::: ex Worked example
You have **$50** in your main wallet and **100 shares** of Yes bought at 30¢. Tomorrow MOONX stops working. Your $50 is still in your wallet on Polygon, under your keys. Your 100 shares still settle on Polymarket: if Yes wins, they're worth 100 × $1 = **$100**. Your backup file and its password still open the wallet, in any compatible wallet software.
:::

## What can still go wrong

::: risk Risks that stay with you
- **The trade itself.** You can lose all the money you put into a trade, plus fees, and no more: there is no leverage. See [can you lose more than you bet](/learn/can-you-lose-more-than-you-bet-on-polymarket). Cheap outcomes are cheap because they usually don't happen.
- **Your backup.** Lose the backup file or its password and the funds are gone for good.
- **Wrong address or network.** A withdrawal to a wrong address can't be reversed. A deposit on another network than Polygon, or in another token than USDC, can be lost.
- **Third parties.** Polymarket, Polygon and smart contracts can fail. USDC can lose its peg or be frozen by its issuer. Savings through Aave carry their own risks.
- **Scams.** MOONX will never ask for your PIN, your backup password or your backup file. Anyone who does is trying to rob you.
:::

There is no deposit insurance on your balance. MOONX is also new software, offered in beta. And it isn't available everywhere: rules vary by country, Polymarket restricts some countries, and MOONX is closed to people in the US, the UK, mainland China, Hong Kong and others listed in the Terms. Check the rules where you live.

For how the keys, the backup file and the PIN fit together, read [your MOONX wallet](/learn/moonx-wallet).

## Sources {src}

1. [MOONX Terms of Service, sections 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 20](/terms)
2. [Polymarket documentation: Builders Program](https://docs.polymarket.com/programs/builders/overview)
3. [Polymarket documentation: pUSD](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/pusd)

# Is Polymarket safe?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/is-polymarket-safe
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Polymarket's contracts run on the Polygon blockchain and have been audited by several firms, including Cantina, Quantstamp and Certora, which lowers but doesn't remove the risk of a bug. The main risks are elsewhere. A result can be disputed and take 4 to 6 days, a thin market can make selling expensive, a wallet you control can't be recovered if you lose access, and scams pose as apps or support. You can also lose your whole stake on any trade.

## What Polymarket does and doesn't do

It helps to know what Polymarket is not:

- **It doesn't set the odds.** Its help center says prices come from supply and demand between users.
- **It isn't the other side of your bet.** The counterparty to each trade is another user, not a house.
- **It doesn't decide results.** Most markets are settled through the UMA oracle ([what is UMA?](/learn/what-is-uma-on-polymarket)).
- **It doesn't guarantee a buyer.** If nobody wants your shares at a fair price, you wait or accept a worse one.

## The risks, one by one

**1. Smart contracts.** Your money and shares sit in contracts on Polygon. Polymarket lists audits from Cantina, Quantstamp, Certora, SigmaPrime, Zellic and Pashov in 2026, and a bug bounty through Cantina. Audits reduce the chance of a flaw. They don't make it zero.

**2. Resolution disputes.** A result follows the market's written rules, not what most people expected. A disputed market goes to a vote of UMA token holders and takes about **4 to 6 days**. A market that can't be answered under its rules can pay **$0.50** per share to both sides ([what happens if a market is unclear?](/learn/what-happens-if-a-polymarket-market-is-unclear)).

**3. Thin markets.** With few orders in the book, the gap between buy and sell prices is wide. When that gap passes 10¢, Polymarket shows the last traded price, which may not be a price you can get ([what is the spread?](/learn/what-is-the-spread-on-polymarket)).

**4. Losing access to your own wallet.** If you control your wallet, nobody can restore it for you. On MOONX, losing the backup file **or** its password means the money is lost for good, by design ([what if I lose my backup file?](/learn/what-if-i-lose-my-moonx-backup-file)).

**5. Sending to the wrong place.** Polymarket's help center warns that transfers to the wrong chain or address cannot be reversed.

**6. Scams posing as apps.** Fake websites, fake apps and fake "support" accounts can copy a real product's name. No real support team needs your backup file, password or PIN. Type the address yourself and check it.

::: ex Worked example
You buy **$40** of Yes at **80¢**: 40 ÷ 0.80 = **50 shares** (before fees).

- Yes wins: 50 × $1 = **$50**.
- No wins: **$0**. The $40 is gone.
- The market is unclear and resolves 50-50: 50 × $0.50 = **$25**.
- You sell early in a thin market where the best bid is 70¢: 50 × 0.70 = **$35**, before fees.

None of these outcomes takes more than the $40 you put in, plus fees ([can you lose more than you bet?](/learn/can-you-lose-more-than-you-bet-on-polymarket)).
:::

## Rules where you live

Polymarket restricts some countries because of regulatory requirements and sanctions. MOONX is not available everywhere either, including the US, the UK, mainland China and Hong Kong (see the Terms). Rules vary by country, so check the rules where you live.

For how MOONX handles your keys and what it can't do with your money, see [is MOONX safe?](/learn/is-moonx-safe). For how a disputed result is settled, read [how Polymarket resolves markets](/learn/how-polymarket-resolves-markets).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: contracts and audits](https://docs.polymarket.com/resources/contracts)
2. [Polymarket documentation: resolution](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/resolution)
3. [Polymarket documentation: prices and order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
4. [Polymarket Help Center: what is Polymarket](https://help.polymarket.com/en/articles/13364060-what-is-polymarket)
5. [Polymarket Help Center: how to deposit](https://help.polymarket.com/en/articles/13369887-how-to-deposit)

7. [MOONX Terms of Service](/terms)

# What are the fees on MOONX?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/moonx-fees
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: MOONX charges 1% of the trade value when you buy and 1% when you sell, shown before you confirm. There is no fee when a market resolves, no subscription, no account fee and no withdrawal fee, and MOONX pays the network (gas) fees. On most markets Polymarket's own taker fee applies as well, and the payment partners that sell you USDC by card show their own fee before you pay.

## What MOONX charges

| What | MOONX fee |
|---|---|
| Buying a shot | 1% of the trade value |
| Selling a shot | 1% of the trade value |
| A market resolving | None |
| Subscription or account fee | None |
| Withdrawing | None |
| Network (gas) fees | Paid by MOONX |

Every fee is included in what you see before you confirm. Because MOONX pays the gas, your wallet never needs to hold another token to trade, add money or withdraw. More on that in [what are gas fees](/learn/what-are-gas-fees).

MOONX's Terms say there is currently no subscription. If one is ever introduced, existing users get at least 30 days' notice, and it will never be needed to reach your wallet or withdraw.

## What others charge

- **Polymarket**, on most markets: the trader whose order fills right away pays `fee = shares × rate × price × (1 − price)`. As a share of the money you spend, that's rate × (1 − price). Rates go from 0 on geopolitics to 0.07 on crypto, with 0.05 on sports and 0.04 on politics.
- **Payment partners** (Stripe and Swapped, through Calm Treasury), if you add money by card, mobile wallet or bank transfer. Their fee is shown before you pay.
- **The exchange or wallet** you send USDC from, or withdraw to, may charge its own fee.

::: ex Worked example
You put **$50** on Yes at **20¢** in a politics market (rate 0.04). You get 50 ÷ 0.20 = **250 shares**.

- MOONX fee: 1% of $50 = **$0.50**
- Polymarket fee: 250 × 0.04 × 0.20 × 0.80 = **$1.60**

Fees to get in: **$2.10**.

**If you hold and Yes wins:** 250 × $1 = $250, with no fee at resolution. Profit after fees: 250 − 50 − 2.10 = **$197.90**. At 20¢, the market sees that as about a 1 in 5 chance.

**If you sell at 40¢:** 250 × 0.40 = $100. MOONX takes 1% = $1.00, Polymarket 250 × 0.04 × 0.40 × 0.60 = $2.40. You receive **$96.60**, a profit of 96.60 − 50 − 2.10 = **$44.50**.

**If No wins:** your shares pay nothing. You lose the $50 and the $2.10 in fees.
:::

## Where MOONX's fee goes

Part of it goes back to users: 25% of MOONX's fee on the trades of people who joined with your link, and 25% when someone trades a market from one of your trades. That comes out of MOONX's share. Nobody pays more because they were invited. Details in [earn with MOONX](/learn/earn-with-moonx).

For every Polymarket rate and the fee at each price, read [Polymarket fees](/learn/polymarket-fees).

## Sources {src}

1. [MOONX Terms of Service, sections 8, 11 and 12](/terms)
2. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)

# What is the minimum bet on Polymarket?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/polymarket-minimum-bet
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Each Polymarket market sets a minimum order size in shares, and 5 shares is common. In practice, Polymarket's order system also rejects an order that fills right away when it's worth under $1. So the smallest instant trade is the larger of 5 × the price and about $1: just over $1 at prices up to 20¢, and 5 × the price above 20¢ ($2.50 at 50¢, $4.50 at 90¢), before fees.

## Two floors

**The share floor.** Polymarket's order book has a setting for each market called the **minimum order size**: the smallest number of shares it accepts in one order. Polymarket's documentation uses **5 shares** as its example, and that was the minimum on every one of the 100 busiest markets we checked on 27 October 2026.

**The dollar floor.** An order that fills right away against the book, called a marketable order, also has to be worth at least $1. This isn't written in Polymarket's official documentation. It's how the order book behaves in practice: developers who send a smaller instant buy get back the error "invalid amount for a marketable BUY order ($X), min size: $1". MOONX's own site states that trades start at just over $1.

When you buy, you choose an amount in dollars. That amount is turned into shares: dollars ÷ price. The order has to clear both floors.

## The smallest trade at each price

| Price | Cost of 5 shares | Smallest instant buy | Shares you get |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1¢ | $0.05 | just over $1 | about 100 |
| 5¢ | $0.25 | just over $1 | about 20 |
| 10¢ | $0.50 | just over $1 | about 10 |
| 20¢ | $1.00 | just over $1 | about 5 |
| 50¢ | $2.50 | $2.50 | 5 |
| 75¢ | $3.75 | $3.75 | 5 |
| 90¢ | $4.50 | $4.50 | 5 |

Before fees, on a 5-share market. At 20¢ or less, the $1 floor is the one that bites. Above 20¢, 5 shares cost more than $1, so the share floor takes over. Either way, the smallest instant trade never costs more than $5.

::: ex Worked example
You want to put **$2** on a market where Yes costs **50¢**. That buys 2 ÷ 0.50 = **4 shares**, one short of a 5-share minimum. You'd need at least 5 × 0.50 = **$2.50**.

Now you want to put **$0.50** on a share at **5¢**. That buys 0.50 ÷ 0.05 = **10 shares**, above the share floor, but the order is worth less than $1, so an instant buy is rejected. You'd need just over **$1**.
:::

## Small trades and fees

Fees don't punish small trades. Polymarket's taker fee is calculated per share: shares × rate × price × (1 − price). There's no fixed charge per order. MOONX's fee is 1% of the trade value, so about 1¢ on a $1 trade. MOONX pays the network (gas) fees on all MOONX transactions, so a small trade doesn't carry a gas cost either.

The spread matters more at small sizes than people expect. You buy at the best ask, which can be a cent above the price on screen. On a 5¢ share, one cent is a fifth of the price.

## Does the same minimum apply on MOONX?

Yes. MOONX passes your order to Polymarket, where it's placed and matched under Polymarket's rules, so both floors apply the same way. MOONX's site puts it simply: trades start at just over $1. A small first trade is a sensible way to learn how buying, selling and payouts work. See [your first trade on MOONX](/learn/first-trade-on-moonx).

Prices also move in fixed steps called ticks, from 0.1 down to 0.0001 depending on the market, so not every price is possible on every market.

For what a given price pays back, read [prediction market odds](/learn/prediction-market-odds).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: place orders](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/place-orders)
2. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)
3. [Polymarket documentation: prices and the order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
4. [MOONX home page: "Starts at just over $1"](https://moonx.fi/)
5. [MOONX Terms of Service, sections 6 and 11](/terms)

# What are gas fees?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-are-gas-fees
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Gas is the unit that measures how much computing work a blockchain transaction takes, and the gas fee is what you pay for it, the gas used multiplied by the price per unit of gas, paid in the network's own token. On Polygon, where Polymarket runs, that token is POL. You pay for the work done even if a transaction fails. On MOONX you never pay gas, because MOONX pays the network fees on all MOONX transactions.

## The definition

A blockchain is run by many computers that check and record every transaction. That work isn't free. **Gas** is the unit that measures how much work a transaction needs, the way litres measure fuel. The **gas fee** is what you pay for it:

`gas fee = gas used × price per unit of gas`

The fee is paid in the network's own token: **ETH** on Ethereum, **POL** on Polygon. Ethereum's documentation gives two reasons the fee exists: it pays for the work, and it stops people from spamming the network or running code that loops forever.

A few details that surprise people:

- **The price moves.** When the network is busy, each unit of gas costs more.
- **A failed transaction still costs gas** for the work done before it failed.
- **Prices are quoted in tiny units.** On Ethereum, gas prices are usually given in **gwei**, one billionth of an ETH.

::: ex Worked example
These numbers are made up, just to show the arithmetic.

A transaction uses **50,000 units** of gas at a price of **30 gwei** per unit.

- Fee: 50,000 × 30 = **1,500,000 gwei**.
- One gwei is 0.000000001 ETH, so the fee is 1,500,000 × 0.000000001 = **0.0015 ETH**.

You would need to hold that ETH in your wallet before sending anything. That is the part that trips up beginners: holding dollars is not enough, you also need the network's token.
:::

## Gas on Polymarket

Polymarket runs on Polygon ([what chain is Polymarket on?](/learn/what-chain-is-polymarket-on)). Its documentation says most of its wallets act through a **relayer** that submits transactions without gas for the user, while a plain wallet acting on its own needs **POL** to pay gas. Gas is separate from Polymarket's trading fee, which is charged on most trades when they match ([Polymarket fees](/learn/polymarket-fees)).

## Gas on MOONX

**MOONX pays the network fees on all MOONX transactions**: adding money to trading, buying, selling, collecting winnings and withdrawing. You never need to buy or hold POL. Your wallet only holds dollars, as USDC on Polygon.

What you do pay on MOONX:

| Cost | Amount |
|---|---|
| Network (gas) fees | $0, paid by MOONX |
| MOONX fee | 1% of the trade value, when buying and when selling |
| Polymarket taker fee | Depends on category and price |
| Card or bank payment partner | Shown before you pay |
| Withdrawal | No MOONX fee |

For example, $20 of Yes at 50¢ on a sports market is 40 shares. The Polymarket fee is 40 × 0.05 × 0.50 × 0.50 = **$0.50**, MOONX's fee is 1% of $20 = **$0.20**, and gas costs you **$0**.

For where your USDC sits and how it moves between your wallet and Polymarket, read [your MOONX wallet](/learn/moonx-wallet).

## Sources {src}

1. [Ethereum.org: gas and fees](https://ethereum.org/en/developers/docs/gas/)
2. [Polymarket documentation: wallets and authentication](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/wallets-auth)
3. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)
4. [MOONX Terms of Service](/terms)

# What are Polymarket rewards and rebates?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-are-polymarket-rewards
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Polymarket has three programs that pay traders back. Liquidity rewards pay traders whose limit orders wait in the book close to the midpoint, scored once a minute and paid daily. Maker rebates return part of the taker fees each day to makers whose orders get filled, from 15% of fees in sports to 25% in politics. The Taker Rebate Program, started on 28 May 2026, gives traders who pay fees a rebate of 3% to 50% depending on 30-day weighted volume. All three pay daily, with nothing paid below $1.

## First, makers and takers

An order that **waits** in the book is a maker order ([what is a limit order?](/learn/what-is-a-limit-order-on-polymarket)). An order that **fills right away** against it is a taker order. On most markets takers pay a fee and makers pay none ([Polymarket fees](/learn/polymarket-fees)). The three programs that pay traders back are built around that split. Polymarket also runs a Referral Program and the [Builders Program](/learn/what-is-a-polymarket-builder) for apps built on it, which this page doesn't cover.

## 1. Liquidity rewards (makers)

Paid to traders who keep limit orders resting in the book.

- Each eligible market sets its own **maximum spread** from the midpoint, **minimum order size** and reward budget, shown in the market's details.
- Orders closer to the midpoint score more. Scores fall to zero at the maximum spread.
- Quoting on **both sides** scores best. One side alone still earns, at a third of the rate. If the midpoint is under 10¢ or over 90¢, only two-sided quotes count.
- The book is sampled once a minute, so up to 24 × 60 = **1,440 samples** a day. Your share of the day's score is your share of that market's rewards.
- Paid daily at **midnight UTC**. Amounts under **$1** are not paid out.

## 2. Maker rebates (makers)

Taker fees fund a daily rebate for makers whose orders get **filled**. The share returned depends on the category:

| Category | Share of taker fees returned |
|---|---:|
| Crypto | 20% |
| Sports | 15% |
| Finance, politics, economics, culture, weather, tech, mentions, other | 25% |
| Geopolitics | No fee, no rebate |

Your part is your filled maker volume, weighted by the same price curve as the fee, compared with all other makers **in that market**. Paid daily in **pUSD**, once you reach **$1**.

## 3. Taker rebates (takers)

Started on **28 May 2026**. Every fee-paying trade earns **weighted volume**:

`wV = trade size × (1 − price) × category weight × any bonus`

Weights: sports 1.0; politics, finance, mentions, tech 1.3; economics, culture, weather, other 1.7; crypto 2.3; geopolitics 0. Your 30-day total sets your tier:

| Tier | 30-day weighted volume | Rebate | One-time bonus |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Bronze | $2,000 | 3% | $10 |
| Silver | $20,000 | 8% | $50 |
| Gold | $200,000 | 18% | $250 |
| Platinum | $1,000,000 | 32% | $1,500 |
| Diamond | $4,000,000 | 44% | $7,500 |
| Obsidian | $10,000,000 | 50% | $25,000 |

The rebate applies only to trades made after you reach a tier, with no backfill. Paid daily at midnight UTC in pUSD, from $1. Polymarket's docs add that third-party integrations using omnibus wallets are not eligible.

::: ex Worked example
You trade sports markets at **50¢**. Each dollar traded earns 1 × (1 − 0.50) × 1.0 = **$0.50** of weighted volume.

To reach Bronze, you need $2,000 of weighted volume in 30 days: $2,000 ÷ 0.50 = **$4,000** of trades. Polymarket's own example: 1,000 politics shares at 40¢ is a $400 trade, worth 400 × 0.60 × 1.3 = **$312** of weighted volume.
:::

::: note Read the fine print
Polymarket can change rates, weights, thresholds and bonuses at any time, and can remove rebates for wash trading or self-matching. None of these programs makes a losing trade a winning one. Check the current pages before counting on a number.
:::

MOONX's own program, which shares part of MOONX's fee with people who bring in other traders, is separate: see [earn with MOONX](/learn/earn-with-moonx).

For what you pay before any rebate, read [Polymarket fees explained](/learn/polymarket-fees).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: liquidity rewards](https://docs.polymarket.com/programs/liquidity-rewards)
2. [Polymarket documentation: Maker Rebates Program](https://docs.polymarket.com/programs/maker-rebates)
3. [Polymarket documentation: Taker Rebate Program](https://docs.polymarket.com/programs/taker-rebates)
4. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)


---

# What are Polymarket Up or Down markets?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-are-polymarket-up-or-down-markets
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Polymarket Up or Down markets ask whether a crypto pair, such as BTC/USD, ends a set time window higher or lower than it started. Both the starting price and the final price come from the same Chainlink time-weighted average price, and the market resolves Up if the final price is equal to or greater than the start, Down if it is lower. They settle without UMA's proposal and dispute process, and they carry the crypto taker fee rate of 0.07.

## How one works

Each Up or Down market names an **asset pair**, a **start time** and a **duration**. Polymarket's documentation gives the example of whether BTC/USD moves Up or Down during a one-hour window. Its liquidity rewards page names other crypto markets, of **5 minutes, 15 minutes and 4 hours**, that also settle on a Chainlink TWAP.

1. At the start, a price is recorded. Polymarket calls it the **price to beat**.
2. At the end of the window, the final price is recorded.
3. If the final price is **equal to or greater than** the price to beat, **Up** wins. If it is lower, **Down** wins.

Each winning share pays $1, each losing share $0, as on any Polymarket market.

## Where the prices come from

Both prices come from the same **Chainlink** stream, a **TWAP**: a time-weighted average price over a defined lookback window. So the final price is an average over a short period, not the price at one exact second.

Because the result follows directly from these observations, these markets resolve without UMA's proposal and dispute process. The same data always gives the same result. Other markets work differently, see [what UMA is on Polymarket](/learn/what-is-uma-on-polymarket).

## The tie rule

A tie goes to **Up**. If the final price is exactly the price to beat, Up wins. It rarely matters, but read it before you buy Down.

## Fees, and why they add up

Up or Down markets are crypto markets, and Polymarket's crypto taker rate is **0.07**, the highest of its categories. At 50¢, that's 0.07 × (1 − 0.50) = **3.5%** of the money you spend.

::: ex Worked example
You buy **$10** of Up at **50¢**: 10 ÷ 0.50 = **20 shares**.

Polymarket fee: 20 × 0.07 × 0.50 × 0.50 = **$0.35**.

If Up wins, you receive $20, a profit of 20 − 10 − 0.35 = **$9.65**. On MOONX, add its 1% fee, $0.10, for a profit of **$9.55**.

Now repeat it **10 times**, $10 each at 50¢, and win exactly half. You get back 5 × $20 = $100 on $100 staked, and you've paid 10 × $0.35 = **$3.50** in Polymarket fees. Breaking even on wins still loses money.
:::

## What to keep in mind

- Price moves over a few minutes are hard to predict. A 50¢ price says the market sees the outcome as close to even.
- Fees are charged on every trade, so many short trades add up fast, as the example shows.
- At a price near 50¢, a win roughly doubles your money, minus fees. Bigger multiples only come from buying a side the market thinks is unlikely.

Full detail on how every kind of market settles is in [how Polymarket markets are resolved](/learn/how-polymarket-resolves-markets).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: resolution](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/resolution)
2. [Polymarket documentation: liquidity rewards](https://docs.polymarket.com/programs/liquidity-rewards)
3. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)
4. [MOONX Terms of Service, section 11: fees](/terms)

# What blockchain is Polymarket on?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-chain-is-polymarket-on
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Polymarket runs on Polygon, a blockchain compatible with Ethereum, with chain ID 137. Its contracts, the pUSD token used for trading and your shares all live there. In practice, money you send directly to a Polygon wallet must go over the Polygon network, because transfers sent to the wrong chain or address cannot be reversed. On MOONX your wallet is on Polygon too, and MOONX pays the network fees.

## The short answer: Polygon

Polymarket's smart contracts are deployed on **Polygon mainnet**, chain ID **137**. That is where:

- your trading money sits, as **pUSD**, Polymarket's dollar token ([what is pUSD?](/learn/what-is-pusd));
- your Yes and No shares are recorded, as tokens in your wallet;
- payouts happen when a market resolves.

Because it's a public blockchain, every trade and every payout leaves a record anyone can check.

## What that means for you

**1. The network matters when you send money.** A wallet address on Polygon looks like an Ethereum address, and exchanges often let you pick from several networks for the same token. Polymarket's help center is blunt: transactions sent to the wrong chain or address "cannot be reversed."

**2. Other chains can still be used on Polymarket.** Polymarket's deposit system gives you separate addresses for Ethereum and other EVM chains, Solana, Bitcoin and Tron. What you send there is bridged and converted to pUSD on Polygon. Each asset has a minimum, for example $20 from Ethereum and $3 from Solana. Polymarket's help center says smaller deposits wait until the total reaches it, while its developer documentation says deposits below the minimum are not processed.

**3. Polygon has its own gas token, POL.** Every on-chain action costs a small network fee, called gas ([what are gas fees?](/learn/what-are-gas-fees)). Polymarket's documentation says most of its wallets act through a relayer that covers gas, while a plain wallet that acts on its own needs POL.

::: ex Worked example
You want to move **50 USDC** from an exchange to your MOONX wallet.

1. In MOONX, copy your wallet address.
2. On the exchange, choose **USDC** and the **Polygon** network.
3. Paste the address and send.

If you picked another network, such as Ethereum, the 50 USDC would not arrive in your MOONX wallet and could be lost. Sending a different token carries the same risk.
:::

## Polygon on MOONX

MOONX wallets live on Polygon, the same network as Polymarket. Your main wallet holds **USDC on Polygon**, and money moves to Polymarket as pUSD when you trade. **MOONX pays the network fees on all MOONX transactions**, so you never need to buy or hold POL.

If you add money by card, mobile wallet or bank transfer, the payment partner delivers USDC on Polygon for you. The network question only comes up when you send crypto yourself.

::: risk One rule
When sending to MOONX from an exchange or another wallet: **USDC, Polygon network**. Anything else can be lost for good, and nobody can reverse a blockchain transfer, MOONX included.
:::

For how your wallet's parts fit together on Polygon, read [your MOONX wallet](/learn/moonx-wallet).

# What does the percentage mean on Polymarket?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-does-the-percentage-mean-on-polymarket
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: The percentage is the price of a Yes share, read as a chance. 64% means a Yes share costs about 64¢ and pays $1 if Yes happens, so traders as a group put the chance near 64%. It's the midpoint between the best buy and sell offers, or the last trade price when that gap is wider than 10¢. The price you actually pay can be a little higher.

## Percentage, price and chance are the same number

A share on Polymarket pays **$1** if its outcome happens and $0 if not. So its price in cents reads directly as a chance in percent:

- **64%** on Yes means a Yes share costs about **64¢**.
- No is then around **36%**, because Yes and No together are worth $1.
- If you're right, each share pays $1. At 64¢ that's 1 ÷ 0.64 = about **1.56x** your money, before fees.

## Where the number comes from

Polymarket shows the **midpoint** between the best bid (the highest price someone will pay) and the best ask (the lowest price someone will sell at). If that gap, the spread, is wider than 10¢, it shows the **last traded price** instead.

When you buy right away, you pay the ask, not the midpoint.

::: ex Worked example
**Busy market.** Best bid 63¢, best ask 65¢. The midpoint is (63 + 65) ÷ 2 = **64¢**, shown as 64%. You buy at **65¢**, so your multiple is 1 ÷ 0.65 = about **1.54x**, not 1.56x.

**Quiet market.** Best bid 40¢, best ask 60¢. The spread is 20¢, wider than 10¢, so the screen shows the last trade, say 45%. Buying now would cost **60¢**, well above the number you see.
:::

On a thin market, check the actual buy price before you confirm. More on this in [what the spread is](/learn/what-is-the-spread-on-polymarket).

## What it doesn't mean

- **It's not a promise.** If the prices are right, things priced at 64% still fail about 36 times out of 100.
- **It's not a poll.** It isn't the share of people who think Yes. It's the price where buyers and sellers with money at stake currently meet.
- **It's not fixed.** It moves with every trade. The chart on a market shows how it changed over time, see [how to read a Polymarket chart](/learn/how-to-read-a-polymarket-chart).

## Markets with many outcomes

For a question like "who will win the election?", each candidate has their own Yes and No shares, and each percentage is that candidate's Yes price. Only one outcome can win, so the percentages tend to add up to roughly 100%, give or take the spread. See [multi-outcome markets](/learn/multi-outcome-markets).

For turning any percentage into a payout, with a full table, read [prediction market odds](/learn/prediction-market-odds).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: prices and the order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
2. [Polymarket documentation: negative risk and multi-outcome events](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/negative-risk)

# What happens if a Polymarket market is unclear?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-happens-if-a-polymarket-market-is-unclear
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: An unclear market is judged on its written rules and the source they name. Polymarket can publish a clarification, called additional context, but it can't change what the market is about. If the question truly can't be answered under its rules, the market resolves 50-50 and every share, Yes or No, redeems for $0.50. A result proposed before the event has really happened can be disputed as too early, and then the proposer loses the bond.

## The rules decide, not the headlines

Every market has written rules under its order book: what counts as Yes, which source is used, and the deadline. When events are messy, the result is judged against those rules. A market can be clear on paper and still feel unclear in real life, so reading the rules before you trade is the best protection.

From there, an unclear case can go four ways.

1. **A clarification.** In rare cases Polymarket publishes "additional context" after trading has started. It's recorded on the blockchain, UMA voters are expected to take it into account, and it **can't change the market's basic intent**. Requests go to the `#market-review` channel on Polymarket's Discord.
2. **A dispute.** If someone thinks a proposed result is wrong, they post a bond and challenge it. A second dispute sends the question to a vote of UMA token holders. This takes about 4 to 6 days in total.
3. **Too early.** If someone proposes a result before the event has actually happened, the proposal can be disputed as too early. If it is, the proposer loses the bond and the market keeps waiting for the real outcome.
4. **50-50.** If the question can't be answered under its rules, the market can resolve 50-50. Polymarket's documentation lists this as "Neither outcome applicable (rare)".

## What a 50-50 result does to your money

Every share pays **$0.50**, whichever side you hold. Whether that's good or bad for you depends only on what you paid.

::: ex Worked example
A market resolves 50-50. Three traders each hold **100 shares**.

- Ana bought Yes at **30¢**: paid $30, gets 100 × $0.50 = **$50**. Gain of $20.
- Ben bought Yes at **80¢**: paid $80, gets **$50**. Loss of $30.
- Cleo bought No at **50¢**: paid $50, gets **$50**. Even, before fees.

Fees paid when buying aren't refunded.
:::

## What you can do

- **Read the rules first.** Check the resolution source and the exact deadline, not just the title.
- **Watch for clarifications** on markets you hold, especially near the deadline.
- **Sell if you're unsure.** You can usually sell your shares at the current bid, if there is a buyer, before the market closes. That can be simpler than waiting through a dispute of 4 to 6 days. See [selling before the result](/learn/sell-before-the-result).

::: note On MOONX
MOONX passes your orders to Polymarket and follows its results. Resolution, including any dispute, clarification, delay or reversal, is handled by Polymarket's process. MOONX can't change, appeal or reverse an outcome.
:::

For the whole process, with bonds, timings and votes, read [how Polymarket resolves markets](/learn/how-polymarket-resolves-markets).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: resolution](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/resolution)
2. [MOONX Terms of Service, section 6](/terms)

# What happens if you lose your MOONX backup file?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-if-i-lose-my-moonx-backup-file
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: If you lose your MOONX backup file or its password, nobody can restore your wallet, MOONX included, and the money in it is lost for good. MOONX keeps no copy of either, by design. The file and the password only work together, so keep the file in two places and the password in a password manager. MOONX will never ask you for them, and anyone who does is trying to steal from you.

## Why nobody can get it back

Your wallet keys are created on your device. They leave it only inside your **backup file**, encrypted with a **password** you choose. That password is never sent to MOONX, so it can't be read, reset or recovered from MOONX's side.

Under MOONX's Terms (section 5), the wallet is in your custody alone. The reason is simple: anyone who could restore your wallet for you could also empty it. MOONX holds neither the file nor the password, so there is nothing to send you, and nothing for anyone to take from MOONX.

The file without the password is useless. The password without the file is useless. Losing **either one** has the same result.

## What you can lose, and what happens

| You lose | What happens |
|---|---|
| Your PIN | An inconvenience: your backup file and password restore you |
| Your phone | Log in elsewhere with your email, upload the file, enter the password, set a new PIN |
| Your backup file | The wallet can't be opened on a new device: the money is lost |
| Your backup password | Same: the file can't be opened, and the money is lost |

Logging out or closing the app doesn't touch your wallet. But only the backup gets you back in on a new device.

::: ex Worked example
You have **$200** in your MOONX wallet, and your phone falls into the sea.

**Case A:** your backup file is on a cloud drive and a USB stick, and its password is in a password manager. You log in on a new phone with your email, upload the file, enter the password and choose a PIN. Your **$200** and your trades are all there.

**Case B:** the file was only on that phone. The **$200** still sits on the Polygon blockchain, but nobody can ever move it again.
:::

## How to keep both safe, today

1. **Save the file in two places** on the day you make it, such as a cloud drive and a USB stick.
2. **Keep the password in a password manager**, not in a note next to the file. Together, the file and the password are the keys to your money.
3. **Treat the password like the only key to a house.** There is no reset link.

::: risk MOONX will never ask
MOONX will never ask for your backup file, your backup password or your PIN, by email, in chat, on Telegram or in the app. Anyone who does is trying to rob you, whatever they claim to be.
:::

This is the trade-off of a [non-custodial wallet](/learn/what-is-a-non-custodial-wallet): nobody can freeze your money, and nobody can rescue it. The full picture is in [your MOONX wallet](/learn/moonx-wallet).

## Sources {src}

1. [MOONX Terms of Service, section 5: your wallet and self-custody](/terms)

# What is a combo on Polymarket?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-is-a-combo-on-polymarket
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: A combo on Polymarket combines two or more outcomes, called legs, into a single pair of Yes and No positions. The combo's Yes pays only if every leg wins, and its No pays if any leg loses. The price doesn't come from the order book. Market makers quote it when you ask, and you accept or let the quote expire. Polymarket's fee rate for combos is 0.05, whatever the categories of the legs.

## The short answer

A **combo** takes outcomes from different markets and joins them into one position. Each outcome is a **leg**. Polymarket's documentation describes a combo's Yes as paying out "when every leg in the combination pays out," and its No as the complement: it pays when the full combination does not.

- A combo has from **2 to 50 legs**.
- Legs must come from markets that are enabled for combos. Not every market is.
- **Contradictory legs** can't be combined. You can't pick both Yes and No on the same outcome.

## How the price is set

A normal Polymarket trade fills against the order book. A combo works by **request for quote**:

1. You choose your legs and an amount, and send a request.
2. Connected market makers have **400 milliseconds** to send a price.
3. You get the best quote and have a few seconds to accept it.
4. If you accept, the trade usually executes (the market maker can have a one-second last look). If no maker quotes, there is no trade.

Because makers set the price, a combo can cost more or less than multiplying the legs' prices together. Treat that product as a rough guide, not the price you will get.

::: ex Worked example
Leg 1: Yes at **60¢**. Leg 2: Yes at **50¢**. If the two are unrelated, both happening has a chance of about 0.60 × 0.50 = **30%**.

Say a maker quotes **30¢**. For **$15** you get 15 ÷ 0.30 = **50 shares**. At the combo rate of 0.05, the fee is 50 × 0.05 × 0.30 × 0.70 = about **$0.53**.

If both legs win, you receive **$50**, a profit of about 50 − 15 − 0.53 = **$34.47**. If either leg loses, you get **$0**. At a 30% chance, that happens about 7 times in 10.
:::

Real quotes depend on the makers, and legs that are linked to each other, where one outcome makes the other more likely, won't follow the simple product.

## Fees and selling

Polymarket's fee table lists a **0.05** rate for combos, and the documentation says every combo uses it, whatever the categories of its legs. When you buy, the quote includes fees in the total. Selling a combo goes through the same quote process, sized in shares, with the amount you receive shown after fees.

When some legs have resolved and others haven't, Polymarket can simplify the position so it keeps only the legs still open.

## What to keep in mind

- Every extra leg makes the combo less likely to win. The bigger payout is the price of that.
- A combo with many legs is a [long shot](/learn/long-shot-trades), with the same risk: most of them lose.
- Check each leg's rules, as on any market. One leg resolving against you is enough to lose.

For events where only one outcome can win, Polymarket has a different structure, explained in [multi-outcome markets](/learn/multi-outcome-markets).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: how combos work](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/combos/overview)
2. [Polymarket documentation: combinatorial positions](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/positions/combinatorial)
3. [Polymarket documentation: combos for requesters](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/combos/requesters)
4. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)
