# What is a limit order on Polymarket?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-is-a-limit-order-on-polymarket
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: A limit order on Polymarket is an order with a price cap when you buy, or a price floor when you sell. If the order book already has a matching offer, it fills right away. If not, it waits in the book until another trader takes it, it expires, or you cancel it. An order that waits and gets filled is a maker order, and Polymarket charges makers no fee.

## The short answer

A **limit order** says: buy at this price or lower, or sell at this price or higher. Polymarket's documentation puts it simply: use one "when price control matters more than immediate execution."

What happens next depends on the book:

- If someone is already selling at your price or better, your order fills right away, like a market order. That part pays the normal taker fee.
- If nobody is, your order **rests in the book** and waits. It can fill all at once, in pieces as different traders take it, or not at all.

A **market order** is the opposite: it fills now against the best offers available, and any part that can't fill is cancelled. It never waits.

## How long it waits

Polymarket has a few options for how long a limit order stays open:

- **GTC** (good till cancelled): stays until it fills or you cancel it.
- **GTD** (good till date): stays until a time you choose. The expiry must be at least 3 minutes ahead.
- **Post-only**: if the order would fill right away, it is rejected instead. This makes sure you only ever add to the book, never take from it.

Your price must follow the market's tick size, the smallest price step it accepts, and your size must meet the market's minimum number of shares. See [the minimum bet on Polymarket](/learn/polymarket-minimum-bet).

On sports markets, Polymarket automatically cancels open limit orders when the game begins. Start times can shift, so the docs advise watching your orders around kickoff.

## Why use one

::: ex Worked example
On a politics market, Yes has a best bid of **34¢** and a best ask of **40¢**. You want 100 shares.

**Buy now:** you pay the ask. 100 × $0.40 = **$40**, plus a taker fee of 100 × 0.04 × 0.40 × 0.60 = **$0.96**. Total about $40.96.

**Limit buy at 35¢:** your order becomes the new best bid and waits. If a seller fills it, you pay 100 × $0.35 = **$35** and no Polymarket fee, because you were the maker.

Difference: $40.96 − $35 = **$5.96**, if it fills. If the price climbs to 50¢ without ever coming back to 35¢, you get nothing, and the trade you wanted is gone.
:::

That trade-off is the whole decision. A limit order gets you a better price or no trade. A market order gets you the trade at whatever the book charges, including the [spread](/learn/what-is-the-spread-on-polymarket) and any [slippage](/learn/what-is-slippage-on-polymarket).

## Makers, fees and rewards

On Polymarket, **makers pay no fee**. Only takers do. Makers can also earn maker rebates, and resting orders close to the midpoint can qualify for liquidity rewards. More in [what liquidity is on Polymarket](/learn/what-is-liquidity-on-polymarket).

On MOONX, you choose Yes or No and an amount, see the price and the cost, and confirm. The full mechanics of the order book are in [how Polymarket works](/learn/how-polymarket-works).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: placing orders, order types and sizes](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/place-orders)
2. [Polymarket documentation: prices and the order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
3. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)
4. [Polymarket documentation: markets and events](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/markets-events)

# What is a non-custodial wallet?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-is-a-non-custodial-wallet
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: A non-custodial wallet is a crypto wallet whose keys only you hold. No wallet provider can move, freeze or spend the money in it, and none can recover it if you lose your keys. One limit: a stablecoin issuer such as Circle can freeze USDC at the token level, whatever wallet holds it. With a custodial account, like an exchange account, the company holds the money and you hold a login. On MOONX, the wallet is created on your device and backed up as one encrypted file with a password you choose, and MOONX never holds either.

## Keys, in plain words

On a blockchain, money sits at an address. A **private key** is what signs a transaction that moves it. Whoever holds the key controls the money, and nobody else can.

- **Custodial:** a company holds the keys for you. You log in to see a balance, and the company moves the money when you ask.
- **Non-custodial:** you hold the keys yourself, on your device. Nobody can move the money without them.

## The difference that matters

| Question | Custodial account | Non-custodial wallet |
|---|---|---|
| Who holds the keys | The company | You |
| Can the company freeze or move your money | Yes | No |
| If the company stops operating | Your balance can be stuck | Your money stays on chain, under your keys |
| If you lose your access | The company can usually reset it | Nobody can recover the keys |

The last row is the price of the other three. A wallet nobody else can freeze is also a wallet nobody else can rescue.

One limit applies to both columns: a stablecoin issuer such as Circle can freeze USDC at the token level, whichever wallet holds it. A non-custodial wallet takes the wallet provider out of the picture, not the issuer of the token.

::: ex Worked example
Two people each hold **$100**. One keeps it in an account at a company that suddenly stops withdrawals: the $100 waits until the company decides. The other keeps it in a non-custodial wallet whose app stops working: the $100 is still at their address, and their key still moves it, from any compatible wallet software. In both cases the amount is the same. What differs is who decides when it moves.
:::

## How MOONX applies it

MOONX is non-custodial software. In practice:

- Your wallet is **created on your device**, and its keys are generated and kept there. MOONX holds no copy and can't move, freeze or access your money.
- Instead of a seed phrase, you keep **one encrypted backup file** and **a password** you choose. Together they bring your wallet back on a new device.
- A **PIN** of 6 to 12 digits approves every trade and money move on each device.
- Withdrawals only go to addresses on your **Payout Wallets** list, a safeguard that runs in your wallet.
- Your funds remain reachable with your Backup through any compatible wallet software, without MOONX (MOONX Terms of Service, section 20).
- MOONX doesn't ask for an ID document to sign up. Its Terms let it ask for verification in some cases, and payment partners may run their own identity checks when you add money.

The responsibility is real: if you lose the backup file or its password, the money is lost for good. See [what happens if you lose your MOONX backup file](/learn/what-if-i-lose-my-moonx-backup-file).

For the full picture of the MOONX wallet, from savings to network fees, read [your MOONX wallet](/learn/moonx-wallet).

## Sources {src}

1. [MOONX Terms of Service, sections 2, 5 and 20](/terms)

# What is a Polymarket builder?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-is-a-polymarket-builder
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: A Polymarket builder is a person, team or company that routes orders from users to Polymarket through its own app. Each order carries the builder's code, which is recorded on-chain, so matched trades count toward the builder's volume. A builder's volume can appear on the public leaderboard at builders.polymarket.com, which ranks the top builders. Builders get gas-free on-chain operations through Polymarket's relayer. MOONX is a Polymarket builder.

## The definition

Polymarket's documentation describes a builder as one that "routes orders from users to Polymarket". In practice, that means an app with its own design and features, whose trades all happen on Polymarket's order book.

The **Builders Program** gives these apps three things:

- **A builder code.** It is attached to every order and written on-chain as part of the signed order. Each matched trade that carries it counts toward the builder's volume.
- **Leaderboard visibility.** A builder's volume can appear on the public leaderboard at **builders.polymarket.com**, which ranks the top builders. It can take up to 24 hours to show.
- **Gas-free operations.** Wallet setup, approvals, orders and position moves go through Polymarket's relayer at no gas cost.

## Builder levels

Polymarket lists three tiers, mostly about how much traffic an app can send:

| Tier | Relayer transactions per day | How you get it |
|---|---:|---|
| Unverified | 100 | Create a builder profile |
| Verified | 10,000 | Apply and be approved by Polymarket |
| Partner | Unlimited | Enterprise level |

Verified builders can also be considered for weekly USDC rewards and grants, subject to approval.

## What it means when you use a builder app

- **Same markets, same order book.** Your order meets other traders on Polymarket, at Polymarket's prices. The market rules and the way results are decided ([what is UMA?](/learn/what-is-uma-on-polymarket)) are the same.
- **Polymarket's fees still apply.** The app may add its own fee on top. Check it before you trade.
- **Your money depends on the app's wallet design.** The builder label is about routing and attribution. Who controls your funds is set by each app's own wallet and terms, so read them.

::: ex Worked example
You buy **$20** of Yes at **50¢** in a sports market on MOONX.

- You get 20 ÷ 0.50 = **40 shares** (before fees).
- The order goes to Polymarket's order book with MOONX's builder code.
- Polymarket's taker fee: 40 × 0.05 × 0.50 × 0.50 = **$0.50**. MOONX's fee, 1% of $20: **$0.20**. Every fee is included in what you see before you confirm.
- Once matched, the trade counts toward MOONX's builder volume. Your shares sit in your own wallet.
:::

## MOONX as a builder

MOONX is a **Polymarket builder**. Every trade you make on MOONX is a real Polymarket trade. MOONX's wallet is non-custodial: it is created on your device, and MOONX can't move, freeze or recover your money ([what is a non-custodial wallet?](/learn/what-is-a-non-custodial-wallet)). MOONX pays the network fees.

For the mechanics underneath every builder app, read [how Polymarket works](/learn/how-polymarket-works).

# What is a shot on MOONX?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-is-a-shot-on-moonx
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: A shot is MOONX's word for a trade: a position in one outcome of a Polymarket market, bought through MOONX. Each share costs between 0 and $1 and pays $1 if your outcome wins, $0 if it loses. A shot that resolves your way is called a Moon. You can sell a shot before the end, and the MOONX feed shows real shots from other users that you can trade from, on the same side or the other one.

## A shot, in plain words

Every Polymarket market asks a question with a clear answer, like "Will this team win on Saturday?". You pick an outcome, Yes or No, and an amount. MOONX buys you shares of that outcome on Polymarket. Those shares are your shot.

Each share trades between 0 and $1. If your outcome happens, each share pays **$1**. If it doesn't, it pays **$0**. The price works like a probability: a share at 25¢ means the market sees about a 25% chance. More in [what the percentage means on Polymarket](/learn/what-does-the-percentage-mean-on-polymarket).

::: ex Worked example
You take a **$5** shot on Yes at **10¢**. You get 5 ÷ 0.10 = **50 shares**. If Yes wins, they pay 50 × $1 = **$50**, which is 10x your money before fees. If No wins, they pay nothing and you lose your $5. At 10¢, the market sees about a 1 in 10 chance: big multiples come from unlikely outcomes, and most of those miss.

Fees: MOONX takes 1% of $5, so $0.05, and Polymarket's own fee applies on most markets.
:::

## Shot, Moon, Eject

- **Shot:** your position. It updates as the price moves.
- **Moon:** a shot that resolves your way. Each share pays $1 in USDC. Any figure showing what a shot would pay if it moons is arithmetic on the current price, not a forecast.
- **Eject:** the button that sells a shot before the end, at the best price on the book. See [how to sell on MOONX](/learn/how-to-sell-on-moonx).

You never have to hold a shot to the end. And the most you can lose on a shot is what you put in, plus fees.

## Shots in the feed

The MOONX feed shows **real trades from MOONX users**. When you see one, you can take the same side or the other one. A shot in the feed is information, not a recommendation: it shows what someone else did, once.

If you trade a market from someone's shot, that user earns 25% of MOONX's fee on your trade. It comes from MOONX's share, so you pay exactly the same fees as anyone else. Your own shots can earn you the same way, as explained in [earn with MOONX](/learn/earn-with-moonx).

Your shots may appear in the feed, on your profile and on cards you share. Shots sit on a public blockchain, so anyone who knows your wallet address can read them.

To take your first one, follow [your first trade on MOONX](/learn/first-trade-on-moonx).

## Sources {src}

1. [MOONX Terms of Service, sections 1, 3, 6, 12 and 13](/terms)
2. [Polymarket documentation: prices and order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
3. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)

# What is expected value in prediction markets?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-is-expected-value-in-prediction-markets
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Expected value, or EV, is what a trade would return on average if you could repeat it many times. For a share that pays $1, EV per share is your estimated chance times $1, minus the price, minus fees. Buying at 40¢ when you think the chance is 50% gives +10¢ per share before fees, and about +8.4¢ after fees on a sports market through MOONX.

## The formula

Call **p** the price you pay for a share (in dollars) and **q** your own estimate of the chance it wins.

- EV per share = **q × $1 − p − fees per share**
- EV per dollar, before fees = **q ÷ p − 1**

If EV is positive, the trade pays on average. If it's zero or negative, it doesn't. When q equals p, EV before fees is zero: you agree with the market, so you have no edge. For a No share, use (1 − q) and the No price.

Fees per share on Polymarket: rate × p × (1 − p). On MOONX, add 1% of p.

## A worked example

::: ex Worked example
Yes trades at **40¢** on a sports market (fee rate 0.05). You think the real chance is **50%**. You put in **$100**: 100 ÷ 0.40 = **250 shares**.

- EV before fees: 0.50 × $1 − $0.40 = **+10¢ per share**, so 250 × $0.10 = **+$25**
- Polymarket fee: 250 × 0.05 × 0.40 × 0.60 = **$3.00**
- MOONX fee: 1% of $100 = **$1.00**
- EV after fees: $25 − $3 − $1 = **+$21**, or about 8.4¢ per share

Check: if Yes wins you get $250, a profit of $250 − $104 = $146. If it loses you lose $104. Half of each: 0.5 × $146 − 0.5 × $104 = **$21**.
:::

## Fees can wipe out a small edge

::: ex Worked example: a thin edge
Yes trades at **60¢** on a crypto market (fee rate 0.07). You think the chance is **62%**.

- EV before fees: 0.62 − 0.60 = **+2¢ per share**
- Polymarket fee: 0.07 × 0.60 × 0.40 = **1.68¢ per share**
- MOONX fee: 1% of 60¢ = **0.6¢ per share**
- EV after fees: 2 − 1.68 − 0.6 = **−0.28¢ per share**

On 100 shares that's about −$0.28. A trade that looked good on paper loses money on average.
:::

The spread works the same way. You buy at the ask, so use the ask as p, not the price shown on screen. Selling before the end adds a second round of fees. Holding to resolution has no fee at the end. More in [Polymarket fees](/learn/polymarket-fees).

## What EV doesn't tell you

- **One trade is not an average.** In the first example you either make $146 or lose $104. The +$21 only shows up across many similar, independent trades.
- **EV is only as good as q.** The price is the market's estimate, built from many traders with money at stake. If your 50% is really 40%, your positive EV is an illusion.
- **Long shots are the classic trap.** A 2026 working paper on 588 million Polymarket trades found that, in aggregate, purchases below 10¢ lost 19.3¢ per dollar. See [long shots on Polymarket](/learn/long-shot-trades).

For turning prices into payouts, with a full table, read [prediction market odds](/learn/prediction-market-odds).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)
2. [Polymarket documentation: prices and the order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
3. [Cardozo, M. and Rivero-Wildemauwe, J. I. (2026), The Favorite-Longshot Bias in Prediction Markets: Evidence from Polymarket, arXiv working paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12878)
4. [MOONX Terms of Service, section 11](/terms)

# What is liquidity on Polymarket?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-is-liquidity-on-polymarket
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Liquidity on Polymarket is how much you can buy or sell close to the current price. It comes from traders who leave limit orders waiting in the order book, called makers. A liquid market has a tight spread and many shares at each price, so you can trade without moving the price much. Polymarket pays liquidity rewards to makers whose orders sit close to the midpoint, on markets with a reward set up.

## The short answer

Every share you buy on Polymarket comes from someone who was willing to sell it. **Liquidity** is how many of those offers are waiting, and how close they are to the current price.

It comes from **makers**: traders who post [limit orders](/learn/what-is-a-limit-order-on-polymarket) and leave them in the book. Takers, who trade right away, use that liquidity up.

## How to tell if a market is liquid

- **The spread is tight.** Polymarket's documentation says it directly: "Tighter spreads mean more liquid markets." On busy markets the gap between best bid and best ask is often a single tick. See [the spread](/learn/what-is-the-spread-on-polymarket).
- **The book is deep.** There are many shares offered at and near the best price, not just a few.
- **The price is a midpoint, not a last trade.** When the spread is wider than 10¢, Polymarket shows the last traded price instead of the midpoint, which is a sign the market is thin.

Liquidity is not the same as [volume](/learn/what-is-volume-on-polymarket). Volume counts trades that already happened. Liquidity is what is available right now.

## Why it matters when you sell

Liquidity matters most on the way out. Two made-up markets, both showing a best bid of 50¢, and you want to sell **200 shares**:

::: ex Worked example
**Market A** has 500 shares bid at 50¢. You sell all 200 there: 200 × $0.50 = **$100**.

**Market B** has 50 shares bid at 50¢, 50 at 47¢ and 100 at 40¢. Your sale walks down the book:

- 50 × $0.50 = $25.00
- 50 × $0.47 = $23.50
- 100 × $0.40 = $40.00

Total: **$88.50**, an average of 88.50 ÷ 200 = about 44¢ a share. Same headline price, **$11.50 less** in your pocket, before fees.
:::

That loss is [slippage](/learn/what-is-slippage-on-polymarket). On thin markets, selling in smaller pieces or waiting with a limit order can help.

## Liquidity rewards

Polymarket pays makers to keep markets liquid. According to its documentation:

- Makers who post resting limit orders are **automatically eligible**.
- Each rewarded market sets its own **maximum spread** from the midpoint and **minimum order size**. Orders outside those limits don't count.
- Orders **closer to the midpoint score higher**. Orders on both sides of the book are favoured. When the midpoint is below 10¢ or above 90¢, orders must be on both sides to score at all.
- The book is sampled once a minute, and rewards are paid **daily at midnight UTC**. Amounts under **$1** are not paid.

Makers also pay no trading fee on Polymarket and can earn maker rebates. More in [Polymarket rewards](/learn/what-are-polymarket-rewards).

On MOONX, the price and cost of a trade are shown before you confirm, and how the order book shapes them is explained in [how Polymarket works](/learn/how-polymarket-works).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: prices and the order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
2. [Polymarket documentation: liquidity rewards](https://docs.polymarket.com/programs/liquidity-rewards)
3. [Polymarket documentation: fees](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/fees)

# What is pUSD on Polymarket?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-is-pusd
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: pUSD (Polymarket USD) is the collateral token used for all trading on Polymarket. It is a standard ERC-20 token on the Polygon blockchain, backed by USDC, with the backing enforced by a smart contract and no algorithmic peg or fractional reserve. Shares are bought with pUSD and a winning share pays 1 pUSD. Polymarket's documentation says that day to day nothing changes for the user, who still loads funds, trades and withdraws.

## pUSD in plain words

pUSD is a digital dollar that only exists to trade on Polymarket. Every share you buy is paid for in pUSD, and every winning share pays out **1 pUSD**. When a Yes buyer at 60¢ is matched with a No buyer at 40¢, their money together creates one Yes share and one No share, a set worth exactly 1 pUSD.

According to Polymarket's documentation, pUSD is:

- **A standard token on Polygon**, the blockchain Polymarket runs on, with 6 decimals.
- **Backed by USDC**, a dollar stablecoin. A smart contract enforces the backing. In the docs' words: "No algorithmic peg, no fractional reserve."
- **Transferable**, but Polymarket says it has no current plans to list it on outside exchanges. It is a settlement tool, not something to trade for itself.

## How money becomes pUSD and back

Two smart contracts do the conversion. One wraps USDC.e (a form of USDC on Polygon) into pUSD. The other unwraps pUSD back into USDC.e. When you deposit from another blockchain, Polymarket's bridge converts the money to pUSD automatically.

Polymarket sums it up this way: "Day to day, nothing changes. You load funds, see a balance, trade, and withdraw." pUSD is the layer underneath.

::: ex Worked example
You move **$20** of USDC into trading. It becomes **20 pUSD**.

You buy Yes at **25¢**. That gets you 20 ÷ 0.25 = **80 shares** (fees left out to keep it simple).

- If Yes wins, the 80 shares pay **80 pUSD**, which can be turned back into USDC and withdrawn.
- If No wins, the 80 shares pay **0 pUSD** and the $20 is lost.
:::

## pUSD on MOONX

On MOONX you never have to handle pUSD yourself. Your main wallet holds **USDC on Polygon**. When you trade, the money you put in play moves to Polymarket as pUSD automatically, and winnings come back to your wallet. MOONX pays the network fees for these moves, so you don't need any other token.

::: note What to check
If you send money to your MOONX wallet from an exchange, send **USDC on the Polygon network**. Other tokens or other networks can be lost. You don't need to send pUSD.
:::

## Is pUSD risky?

pUSD depends on USDC keeping its value and on the smart contracts working as written. Polymarket's contracts have been audited by several firms, which lowers that risk without removing it. For a wider look at what can go wrong, see [is Polymarket safe?](/learn/is-polymarket-safe).

For the full picture of how money, shares and payouts fit together, read [how Polymarket works](/learn/how-polymarket-works).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: Polymarket USD (pUSD)](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/pusd)
2. [Polymarket documentation: deposit](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/bridge/deposit)
3. [Polymarket documentation: contracts and audits](https://docs.polymarket.com/resources/contracts)
4. [MOONX Terms of Service](/terms)

# What is slippage on Polymarket?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-is-slippage-on-polymarket
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Slippage on Polymarket is the difference between the best price in the order book and the average price your order actually gets. A market order fills against the cheapest offers first, and if there aren't enough shares at that price, it moves on to the next, more expensive ones. The larger your order compared with what's in the book, the worse your average price. Small orders on busy markets see little or none.

## The short answer

An order book is a queue of offers at different prices. A **market order** takes the best offer first. If that offer is smaller than your order, it takes the next one, then the next. Traders call this **walking the book**.

Each step up costs a little more, so your average price ends up above the best price you saw. That difference is **slippage**. Polymarket's documentation warns that "large orders may move the price significantly" and advises: "Always check orderbook depth before trading in size."

## A worked example

The order book below is **made up for this example**. It shows the sell offers (asks) for Yes on an imaginary market.

| Ask price | Shares offered |
|---:|---:|
| 40¢ | 100 |
| 42¢ | 150 |
| 45¢ | 200 |

::: ex Worked example
You send a market order to buy **$148** of Yes. The best ask is 40¢, so you might expect 148 ÷ 0.40 = **370 shares**.

Here is how it actually fills, before fees:

- 100 shares at 40¢ = $40. $108 left.
- 150 shares at 42¢ = $63. $45 left.
- 100 shares at 45¢ = $45. Done.

You get 100 + 150 + 100 = **350 shares**. Your average price is 148 ÷ 350 = about **42.3¢**, not 40¢.

That's **20 fewer shares**. If Yes wins, you collect $350 instead of $370. Your order also cleared the two cheapest levels, so the next buyer now faces a best ask of 45¢.
:::

Selling works the same way in reverse: a large sale fills against the highest bids first, then lower ones.

## What limits the damage

On Polymarket, a market order for a buy is set in dollars and a sell in shares. Market orders never wait in the book: any part that can't fill is cancelled. Some order types fill everything or nothing (FOK), others fill what they can and cancel the rest (FAK). Polymarket's tools also let an order set a worst acceptable price, so a buy can't cross above it.

In practice:

- **Size to the book.** If your order is small compared with the shares offered at the best price, slippage is close to zero.
- **Prefer busy markets.** More resting orders means more shares at each price. See [what liquidity is on Polymarket](/learn/what-is-liquidity-on-polymarket).
- **Use a limit order** on Polymarket directly when price matters more than speed. See [limit orders](/learn/what-is-a-limit-order-on-polymarket).
- **Split a large sale** into smaller ones over time on a thin market.

## On MOONX

MOONX shows the price and the cost before you confirm. The [Eject button](/learn/how-to-sell-on-moonx) sells at the best price on the book, but on a thin or fast-moving market the price can come out different, and a sale can fill partly, late or not at all. Slippage adds to the [spread](/learn/what-is-the-spread-on-polymarket) and to fees, which are explained in [Polymarket fees](/learn/polymarket-fees).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: prices and the order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
2. [Polymarket documentation: placing orders, order types and sizes](https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/place-orders)
3. [MOONX Terms of Service](/terms)

# What is the spread on Polymarket?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-is-the-spread-on-polymarket
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: The spread on Polymarket is the gap between the best bid, the highest price a buyer offers, and the best ask, the lowest price a seller accepts. Buying right away fills at the ask and selling right away fills at the bid, so a buy followed by an instant sell loses the spread. The price displayed is the midpoint of the two, unless the spread is wider than 10¢, in which case Polymarket shows the last traded price.

## The short answer

Every Polymarket market has an order book with two sides:

- **Bids**: buy orders. The best bid is the highest price someone will pay.
- **Asks**: sell orders. The best ask is the lowest price someone will accept.

The **spread** is best ask − best bid. Polymarket's documentation adds one line worth remembering: "Tighter spreads mean more liquid markets."

The headline price on a market is the **midpoint** between the two. If the spread is wider than 10¢, Polymarket shows the last traded price instead.

## What the spread costs you

When you buy right away you pay the ask, which is above the midpoint. When you sell right away you get the bid, which is below it. So a round trip costs the full spread, before any fee.

::: ex Worked example
Yes has a best bid of **34¢** and a best ask of **40¢**. The spread is **6¢** and the market shows **37¢**.

You put **$20** in at 40¢ and get 20 ÷ 0.40 = **50 shares**. A minute later, nothing has changed and you sell at 34¢: 50 × $0.34 = **$17**.

You lost **$3**, or 15% of your stake, before fees, without the market moving at all.
:::

## Why cheap shares feel it most

What matters is the spread compared with the price. On a long shot with a bid of 4¢ and an ask of 6¢, the spread is only 2¢. But the midpoint is 5¢, and you pay 6¢: that's 1¢ over the midpoint on a 5¢ share, or **20% more** than the price shown. On a 50¢ share, paying 1¢ over the midpoint is 2% more.

Fees follow the same pattern, so long shots carry the highest costs to get in and out. More in [long shot trades](/learn/long-shot-trades).

## When the displayed price misleads

On a quiet market the spread can be wide. Say the best bid is 20¢, the best ask is 45¢ and the last trade was at 40¢. The spread is 25¢, wider than 10¢, so the market shows **40¢**, the last trade. If you hold shares and sell right now, you get **20¢**, half of what the screen suggests.

## How to keep it small

- Trade busy markets. On active ones the spread is often a single tick.
- Look at the price on the buy or sell button, not the headline number. MOONX shows the price and the cost before you confirm.
- On Polymarket directly, a [limit order](/learn/what-is-a-limit-order-on-polymarket) lets you wait for your price instead of paying the spread.
- Trade smaller amounts on thin markets, where a large order also walks the book. See [slippage](/learn/what-is-slippage-on-polymarket).

The full picture of bids, asks and the price you pay is in [how Polymarket works](/learn/how-polymarket-works).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: prices and the order book](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/prices-orderbook)
2. [Polymarket documentation: market details](https://docs.polymarket.com/market-data/market-details)

# What is UMA on Polymarket?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-is-uma-on-polymarket
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: UMA is an optimistic oracle, a system that brings real-world answers onto a blockchain. On Polymarket, anyone can propose a market's result by posting a bond, typically $750 in pUSD. If nobody disputes it within 2 hours, the result is final. If it is disputed twice, UMA token holders vote on the answer through UMA's Data Verification Mechanism (DVM), and the whole process takes about 4 to 6 days.

## UMA in one paragraph

A blockchain can't see the news. It needs someone to tell it who won an election or a match. That someone is called an **oracle**. UMA describes itself as a "decentralized truth machine": an optimistic oracle and dispute system that brings any kind of data on-chain. "Optimistic" means an answer is accepted unless someone challenges it. Prediction markets are one of the uses UMA lists, alongside bridges and insurance.

## How UMA settles a Polymarket market

1. **A proposal.** After the event, anyone can propose the result. They post a **bond**, typically **$750 in pUSD**.
2. **A 2-hour challenge window.** Anyone who thinks the proposal is wrong can dispute it by posting a bond of the same size.
3. **No dispute:** the result stands. The proposer gets the bond back plus a reward.
4. **First dispute:** the proposal is thrown out and a new round of proposals starts.
5. **Second dispute:** the question goes to UMA's **DVM**. After a debate period of 24 to 48 hours, where evidence is posted in UMA's public Discord, UMA token holders vote. The vote takes about 48 hours.

Polymarket's documentation puts the undisputed case at about 2 hours after the proposal and the disputed case at about **4 to 6 days**.

## Why the bond matters

The bond is what makes lying expensive. A wrong or premature proposal loses the whole bond. Whoever wins a dispute gets their own bond back plus **half** of the loser's.

::: ex Worked example
A proposer posts **$750** saying Yes won. A disputer posts **$750** saying No. The question goes to a vote, and voters side with the disputer.

- The disputer gets back $750 + ($750 ÷ 2) = **$1,125**, a gain of **$375**.
- The proposer loses the full **$750**.

If voters had sided with the proposer, the numbers would be reversed.
:::

## Who are the voters?

People who hold the **UMA token**. UMA's documentation says token holders vote on disputes and upgrades and earn rewards for honest participation. They judge the question against the market's written rules, plus any "additional context" Polymarket has published on-chain, which can clarify a market but not change its basic intent.

::: note What this means for you
Polymarket does not pick winners, and neither does any app built on it. If a result is disputed, your shares stay in your wallet and nothing is paid until the market resolves. You can follow proposals and disputes on UMA's public oracle portal. Read the rules of a market before you trade, since that is what the voters judge.
:::

Some markets skip UMA entirely: short crypto Up or Down markets settle automatically from a Chainlink price feed ([what are Up or Down markets?](/learn/what-are-polymarket-up-or-down-markets)).

For the full process, the rare outcomes and what happens when you win, read [how Polymarket resolves markets](/learn/how-polymarket-resolves-markets).

## Sources {src}

1. [Polymarket documentation: resolution](https://docs.polymarket.com/concepts/resolution)
2. [UMA documentation](https://docs.uma.xyz/)
3. [UMA Oracle Portal](https://oracle.uma.xyz/)


---

# What is volume on Polymarket?

URL: https://moonx.fi/learn/what-is-volume-on-polymarket
Updated: 2026-10-27

Short answer: Volume on Polymarket is the amount traded on a market over a period, such as the past 24 hours or since the market opened. It measures activity, so the same shares bought and sold ten times count ten times. It is different from open interest, the value held in positions that are still open, and from liquidity, the orders waiting in the book. High volume usually means an active market, but it says nothing about which side is right.

## The short answer

**Volume** is a running total of trades. Every time shares change hands, the trade adds to the market's volume. Polymarket's market data includes, for example, a figure for "trading volume over the past 24 hours."

Volume tells you a market is busy. Busy markets tend to have more orders in the book, which usually means a tighter [spread](/learn/what-is-the-spread-on-polymarket) and less [slippage](/learn/what-is-slippage-on-polymarket) when you trade.

## Volume is not money at stake

The same shares can be traded again and again, and every trade adds to volume.

::: ex Worked example
100 Yes shares change hands **10 times** in a day, each time at about **50¢**.

Volume in dollars: 10 × 100 × $0.50 = **$500**. Volume in shares: 10 × 100 = **1,000 shares**.

But they are still the same 100 shares. Whoever holds them at the end gets $1 each if Yes wins, so **$100**. The volume figure is five times that.
:::

The number closer to "money at stake" is **open interest**. Polymarket's documentation describes it as the value currently held in outstanding positions, in USDC.

## Three numbers people mix up

| Measure | What it counts |
|---|---|
| Volume | Trades that already happened, over a period |
| Open interest | Value held in positions that are still open |
| Liquidity | Orders waiting in the book right now |

A market can have huge volume and thin liquidity: lots of trading earlier, few orders now. It can also have deep liquidity and little volume: plenty of orders waiting, but few people trading. More on the third in [what liquidity is on Polymarket](/learn/what-is-liquidity-on-polymarket).

## Why numbers don't always match

Polymarket's data documentation counts volume in different ways for different purposes. Some figures are in shares, some count both sides of each trade, and some count only the side that took the order. Two places can therefore show different totals for similar activity. Treat volume as a sign of how active a market is, not as an exact amount of money.

Apps that send orders to Polymarket through its Builders Program, such as MOONX, can also have their volume credited to them on builders.polymarket.com. See [what is a Polymarket builder?](/learn/what-is-a-polymarket-builder).

## What volume doesn't tell you

- **Which side is right.** Volume is the same whether buyers or sellers were correct.
- **That the price is accurate.** Busy markets often price well, but not always. See [are prediction markets accurate](/learn/are-prediction-markets-accurate).
- **Who is trading.** One large trader can create a lot of volume.

How prices turn into probabilities is covered in [prediction market odds](/learn/prediction-market-odds).
